#7771. What Makes a Lucky Dog? | Heroes of the Pet World

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Maybe it is having a family that loves them. Maybe it is a warm bed, a full bowl, and a safe place to sleep. Or maybe luck is something a little more fundamental: having people who see you as an individual and take the time to understand what you need.

At Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption Center near Lake Chapala, Mexico, the dogs may still be waiting for permanent homes, but in the meantime, they are surrounded by caring people who show up for them day after day.

At Lucky Dog, everyone has a unique way to help and collaborate.

Some volunteers walk dogs. Others train them, clean their enclosures, help with fundraising, or coordinate veterinary care. Some foster dogs in their homes. Others help with the less visible work that keeps the center running.

When I visited Lucky Dog, I arrived with Mark and Nancy. Mark helped build the Thursday volunteer group, bringing together people who wanted to help in different ways.

âI've gotten to know a lot of people who want to help, and somehow Thursday became our day. We have our group, and everybody has something they can do. You don't have to do everything. You just have to show up and help with what you can.â

Mark has an injured knee, and at the moment, he cannot walk the long distances over cobblestone roads around the center, but he and Nancy have their own important role. They bring chairs into the enclosures and spend about 20 minutes with the dogs, offering pats, treats, kind words, and ear scratches. The dogs happily settle in beside them.

Different volunteer groups cover each day of the week. Some take dogs for walks, while others help with training, cleaning, maintenance, administration, or fundraising.

That Thursday, each person simply did what they came to do. For the dogs, every part of that effort is what makes them feel lucky.

During the day, the dogs stay in pairs in larger enclosures. They are taken out for long walks or playtime in the larger garden areas around the center. In the mornings and evenings, Valentin, one of only two paid workers at the rescue, moves the dogs between their daytime and nighttime enclosures and feeds them breakfast and dinner. During the day, volunteers help with walks, playtime, training, and puppy lunchtime.

At night, the dogs return to smaller individual enclosures.

When a dog needs medical attention, a veterinarian comes to the center to examine and treat them. Volunteers then follow the veterinarian's instructions and continue treatment.

From Valentin's morning and evening routine to the volunteers who walk, train, feed, and care for the dogs, many people contribute to a Lucky Dog's day.

The roots of today's Lucky Dog Rescue go back to 2001, when Geoffrey Kaye and Lourdes Avila started an animal shelter in Riberas del Pilar. When the shelter closed in 2012, the commitment to helping the area's dogs continued. Volunteers regrouped with veterinarian Dr. Antonio Ladron, and in December 2012, Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption opened its doors.

Since then, the center has continued caring for abandoned and abused dogs while helping prepare them for permanent homes.

In 2025, Lucky Dog took in 23 dogs and placed 23 through adoption or transfer. Approximately 35 new volunteers joined, with around 30 committing to weekly shifts. The center's intended capacity is 22 dogs, yet its average monthly census was close to 30 during the year.

Those numbers give you some idea of the work happening behind every individual dog.

Spicy is dog-reactive and needs to be housed separately from other dogs. Mark has developed a close relationship with her, and she has a very clear opinion about where his attention should go.

âSpicy loves me, and she is not happy when she sees me go into a different enclosure to pet another dog,â Mark said. âI have to do it in a way that I hide from her so she canât see or she won't stop barking.â

It is a sweet story, but it also shows why understanding each dog's personality matters.

Hope Procops, who works as a groundskeeper and guard at Lucky Dog, understands how important volunteers are to organizations like this. Itâs not just about the day-to-day tasks. Itâs about looking after the dogs in their care and preparing them for life beyond the shelter. She says the goal of Lucky Dog Rescue is âto ensure all the dogs in our care are kept healthy, loved, socialized, and given the best chance to find their forever homes.â

Camille Short is in charge of training volunteers and dogs at Lucky Dog. Her approach goes beyond teaching basic commands. The goal is to help dogs develop skills that can help them succeed in a home.

Three young siblings, Sasha, Stephanie, and Sergio, were already showing how quickly puppies can learn. They knew how to sit and lie down on command, and were learning to walk with their harnesses. They were highly motivated by treats and, judging by the puppy kisses, equally enthusiastic about people.

Two of the puppies, Stephanie and Sergio, have already been chosen by families; their adoption papers are signed and ready. Sasha remains available for adoption.

As for Spicy, she arrived at Lucky Dog in 2022 and has been waiting for her new home ever since. Initially anxious and mistrustful, she has come a long way with the daily attention and interactions she receives from volunteers. Now, Spicy is looking for a confident new best friend.

âEverything nice with a little bit of spice,â says Camille of Spicy. âShe loves people and attention but is selective about her four-legged friends.â

Some dogs find their people quickly. Others need more time, medical care, or someone who understands their particular personality. Until then, their days continue with walks, play, veterinary care, clean enclosures, treats, kind words, and volunteers who take the time to understand them.

Vice President of Lucky Dog Rescue, Darryl Painter, describes the mission as:

âImproving animal welfare in Lake Chapala via rescue, adoption, community, and fostering.â

The sense of community was tangible during my visit, but perhaps what stayed with me most was how much we humans and dogs have in common. We are all sentient beings, and in our own ways, we all need to be acknowledged, accepted for who we are, and given the opportunity to love and be loved.

At Lucky Dog, those needs are met in many different ways. A walk, a clean enclosure, a treat, a kind word, or simply having someone take the time to know an individual dog.

Not just having people who care for them, but having people who take the time to know them.

And that is something anyone can do. Whether it is volunteering, fostering, sponsoring, or simply offering time and attention, there is a way to help.

Someone opens an enclosure.Someone picks up a leash.Someone brings a treat.

And perhapsâ¦that is what makes these dogs lucky.

#7770. 23 Cheerful Houseplants That Bloom in Winter

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

Published Nov 23, 2026 3:34 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Winter is a long season of brown lawns, bare trees, and frost-covered shrubs. Our feeling is that if we can’t get color and cheer in outdoor beds this time of year, we may as well cultivate some color indoors. Poinsettias are common, colorful blooms for this season, but aren’t for everyone because they’re toxic to pets, according to the ASPCA. But who says your wintertime plant picks have to be Christmas-themed, or even red? Try these cheerful houseplants on for size, or gift them to your nearest and dearest this season.

Typically a summer bloomer, jasmine can bloom during the winter, adding sweet fragrance to indoor spaces. To encourage rebloom the following year, give it a time-out in the fall in a room that is completely dark at night. Exposure to street light or indoor lighting will interrupt the cycle. Give this nontoxic plant a trim once it blooms, since jasmine tends to get leggy.

From December to April, cyclamen, which can bloom for weeks, sends up lightly fragrant flowers above heart-shaped, silver-marbled foliage. After flowering, the plant loses its leaves and dies back for the summer. Some owners might be tempted to toss spent cyclamens into the trash, but take note: The plant is not dead, just dormant. Continue to water it once in a while and when temperatures cool, it will start growing again. Cyclamen is toxic and should be kept away from cats, dogs, and kids.

These striking succulent houseplants have been popular holiday gifts since the 1800s. Although named for its cactus-like foliage, Christmas cactus needs a little more water than its name suggests. Getting this nontoxic plant to rebloom takes a bit of coaxing in the form of light and temperature control, but it’s so worth it.

In mid-October, start giving the plant long nights of total darkness, 13 hours or more, in temperatures between 55 and 65 degrees, to trigger flower bud production. When buds appear, put the plant back in a sunny indoor location.

Despite their odorous reputation, paperwhites are a perfect pick-me-up plant, provided you steer clear of ‘Ziva’, a common (and smelly) variety that can quickly stink up an entire room. Opt for other paperwhites like ‘Cheerfulness’ and ‘Erlicheer’, which have a less-offensive aroma. Paperwhites don’t require prechilling and are easy to spot in late fall at big-box stores or online from specialty bulb companies. This plant, too, should be kept away from pets and kids, since it is toxic.

Rosemary probably won’t bloom, but the scent alone is uplifting enough. The plant is easy enough to procure during the holidays and can often be found in playful topiary shapes, including that of a Christmas tree. Place it in a sunny kitchen window where it can do double duty as decoration and culinary herb.

While rosemary isn’t harmful to pets or people in normal quantities, if your cat takes an outsize liking to the plant, move it out of reach, as it can be irritating in large quantities.

One of the most interesting succulents around, desert rose grows in a mini tree shape and produces stunning flowers. As you would do for other succulents, water desert rose sparingly. Thick stems give rise to flowers in solid colors—some varieties even have striping—that bloom throughout the year.

After flowering, it’s common for the plant to shed its leaves until new growth emerges in the summer, so don’t give up on it. This is another one to keep away from pets and kids as it is poisonous, particularly to cats.

They get a bad rap for being fussy, but growing orchids is actually pretty simple, provided you offer them bright but indirect light and ample humidity. Water orchids thoroughly and allow them to dry out between waterings. Blooms last for months, so it’s best to choose a plant with buds that haven’t yet opened to get as much longevity out of them as possible. These beauties are nontoxic and safe for households with pets and kids.

Crane’s 4-in-1 Drop Ultrasonic Cool Mist Humidifier is compact, budget-friendly, and humidifies houseplants without making the home feel damp.

Situate the diminutive, nontoxic African violet plant in bright, indirect light and enjoy months of continuous flowering in shades of red, white, purple, and everything in between. Set yourself up for gardening success by picking up a specialized African violet pot with a slow-release wicking reservoir in the bottom that prevents damage to the leaves from overhead watering.

Give them bright, indirect light and plenty of humidity and you’ll enjoy a flower frenzy all winter long from indoor begonias. Dry air may be the norm at this time of year, but it’s a death knell for begonias, so set your plant on a shallow tray of water filled with pebbles to humidify the air around it. As much as they like water, too much of a good thing can be harmful. It’s best to water when the plant shows signs of thirst, such as drooping leaves. While begonias are not toxic to humans, they are toxic to pets.

A peace lily can add verdant height (up to 6 feet, in fact) to a drab corner of your home this winter. Several white flag-like flowers, which are really spathes, grace this beautiful but unpredictable plant. It can be hard to determine when and if a peace lily will flower, but it tends to send up stems in February, provided it receives sufficient bright, indirect light. Keep this toxic plant away from pets and kids.

One of the more unusual and upright houseplants, flowering maple blooms almost nonstop. Palmate maple-like leaves and pendulous flowers resembling Chinese lanterns make for a display that will invite plenty of comments. The variegated leaves of certain varieties up the interest, but variegated and non-variegated leaves can be irritating to skin so you might want to wear gloves while working with this plant. Flowering maple is nontoxic to pets.

Amaryllis bulbs produce spectacular trumpet-shaped flowers. Timing is everything with this plant: Bulbs should be planted approximately 6 weeks before you want flowers. Once the flowering stops, snip the stalk a few inches above the bulb.

To encourage rebloom, remove the bulb from the soil in September and keep it in a cool, dark environment for 2 months before repotting. Think carefully about where you’ll place amaryllis: It can cause severe gastrointestinal distress to pets and people.

Like amaryllis and Christmas cactus, clivias need a chilling period to trigger the development of clusters of orange or yellow lily-like flowers. With no need for high humidity, clivia is perfectly suited to indoor life and will survive the winter in a bright, north-facing window. Kaffir lily contains small amounts of the alkaloid lycorine, which is toxic to humans and pets if consumed in large quantities.

Not to be confused with bleeding heart plant (Dicentra spectabilis), bleeding heart vine is a beautiful climbing plant that produces long-lasting clusters of pink or partly red flowers when placed in a sunny window. Give it a trellis or support to climb, and prune back hard after flowering to keep it under control. Don’t worry about pets and kids getting close; this one’s nontoxic.

One of the easiest houseplants to grow and find, kalanchoe tosses out clusters of flowers in deeply saturated hues. The trick is preventing the tropical succulent from becoming too leggy. Pinch it back after flowering and a rebloom should be close behind. Keep this one away from pets and kids, as it is toxic.

Enjoy large daisy-like flowers indoors with cineraria. Compact clusters of daisy-like flowers sit atop large dark green leaves. Flowers can be red, purple, blue, or white, and each flower has a center eye surrounded by a small white ring. Purchase plants with plenty of buds to get the most out of the bloom period, and keep this poisonous plant away from pets and children.

What many consider a flower is really a spathe that emerges from the plant in hues of red, pink, white, and variegated colors. Each spathe displays a contrasting white or yellow flower spike within. Anthurium prefers bright light and high humidity, which may be challenging in a heated home. Place the plant on a shallow pebble-and-water-filled tray, away from kids and pets, to increase the humidity.

Not to be confused with hardy azaleas, greenhouse azaleas are meant to be grown indoors and will not survive if planted in the garden. Select plants with plenty of unopened buds to increase the amount of time you can enjoy its blooms, and be sure not to let the soil dry out. Swallowing large quantities of this plant can spell trouble for pets and humans, so if your dog is a habitual plant snacker, keep azaleas safely away.

Traditionally grown as a perennial, today’s gloxinias are bred to produce masses of blooms without regard for the long-term health of the plant. By the time they’ve finished flowering, the plant simply has nothing left. For this reason, it’s just as well to think of this nontoxic plant as an annual and treat it well while it’s in bloom: keep it in bright, indirect light, water it enough to keep the soil moist, and feed it with a high-phosphorus liquid plant food every 2 weeks.

As the name implies, the flowers on this columnea resemble small goldfish in shades of red, orange, or yellow. Trailing dark green foliage makes the goldfish plant an excellent choice for a hanging planter in bright light. As with African violets, avoid getting water on its leaves, which will cause browning and, in some cases, fungal problems. If your cats are tempted by the goldfish plant, as they might be by actual goldfish, worry not: This plant is harmless to pets.

Add a taste of the tropics to your indoor winterscape with lipstick plant, a vining beauty that looks fantastic in a hanging basket or cascading down a tall piece of furniture. The red, tubular flowers of this nontoxic plant are an exciting and vibrant contrast to its glossy dark green foliage. The plant prefers bright, indirect sunlight and temperatures of 65 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit. It appreciates a bit of humidity, so keep a spray bottle handy, and also apply a slow-release fertilizer once a month.

The leaves of this brightly hued plant resemble those of a shamrock, though they’re much larger and they’re purple. This South American native also produces delicate five-petaled flowers in white or pink that show off during the day but button up at night. Oxalis likes humidity and temperatures of 65 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit. Keep purple shamrock plants in bright direct light, but out of reach of pets and children, as it is toxic and can be quite irritating and even dangerous if ingested.

If you can get past this succulent’s thorniness and toxicity, crown of thorns makes an intriguing addition to a houseplant collection. Its thick, thorn-covered stems support clumps of 2- to 6-inch-long medium-green leaves topped by clusters of small pink, white, or yellow flowers that bloom year-round. Put it in a sunny spot and fertilize it monthly. Note that this is a good plant for those who are stingy with the watering can, since it doesn’t mind drying out. It’s not good, however, for households with pets or kids, as it’s prickly and poisonous.

We’ll help you set up your first garden—whether that’s a few pots on your patio, a raised bed, or an in-ground plot out back—and select the right plants for your soil and region.

#7766. Two Ginger Brothers Became the First Documented Cases of Marfan Syndrome in Cats

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Cats come in all shapes and sizes. Some have legs that seem a little too long for their bodies, others have ears big enough to pick up satellite signals, and a few look like they haven't quite grown into themselves yet.

But when Gary and Shaggy were kittens, their disproportionately long limbs turned out to be more than an unusual-looking but perfectly charming physical trait. The two brothers would eventually become the first domestic cats confirmed to have Marfan syndrome through genetic testing; not exactly what any cat owner would expect when bringing home a pair of kittens.

As the cats grew, veterinarians identified abnormalities affecting their eyes and enlargement of the aorta, the major blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart. Researchers at Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine and the Baker Institute for Animal Health worked with veterinary and genetic specialists to investigate what was going on.

Their long limbs were one clue. The eye abnormalities and enlarged aortas added two more. Slowly, the pieces of the puzzle began to fit together, pointing researchers toward Marfan syndrome, a rare inherited disorder far better known in human medicine than in veterinary practice. Genetic testing confirmed the connection, uncovering what made these two brothers so unusual.

Marfan syndrome affects connective tissue, the body's natural support system. This tissue helps give structure and strength to the bones, ligaments, skin, eyes, and blood vessels. When something goes wrong with this system, the effects can show up in several different ways.

In humans, the condition often causes unusually long limbs and fingers, a tall, slender build, eye abnormalities, and potentially serious cardiovascular complications.

Abraham Lincoln was famously tall and lanky, which has led to speculation that he may have had Marfan syndrome. No one can say for sure, though. Turns out, even Honest Abe left a few medical mysteries behind!

For Olympic volleyball player Flo Hyman, long limbs gave her an edge on the court. However, her life was tragically cut short, dying at age 31 from cardiac complications from Marfan syndrome.

One of the genes involved in Marfan syndrome is called FBN1. It contains the instructions for producing fibrillin-1, a protein that helps maintain the structure and function of connective tissues throughout the body.

When that gene doesn't work as it should, the effects can extend well beyond a person's or animal's appearance. As the gorgeous ginger duo, Gary and Shaggy, began showing signs similar to those seen in humans with Marfan syndrome, their veterinary team started to wonder if cats could also suffer from the same condition.

Genetic sequencing revealed that Gary and Shaggy both carried two altered copies of FBN1. In other words, they had inherited the mutation from both parents.

In humans, Marfan syndrome typically develops when a person inherits one disease-causing copy of the gene. Having two altered copies is exceptionally rare and can be associated with more severe disease.

So the brothers presented researchers with an interesting puzzle.

Their particular genetic variant didn't completely prevent the gene from functioning. Instead, it partially disrupted how the gene's instructions were processed, allowing some normal fibrillin-1 function to remain, which may explain why Gary and Shaggy survived into adulthood despite carrying two copies of the variant.

Their genetic instructions weren't simply switched on or off; it was something in between, which may help explain why the brothers developed the way they did.

Genes rarely behave like a tidy set of instructions. The effects of a genetic change depend on the specific variant involved and how it affects the resulting protein. Sometimes, a seemingly insignificant variation can have catastrophic consequences, altering the way the body functions.

The case of Gary and Shaggy is undeniably rare, and Marfan syndrome is unlikely to find its way onto the list of common feline diseases. However, in diagnosing and documenting the condition, veterinarians have something they didn't have before: a confirmed case of feline Marfan syndrome to help recognize, investigate, and compare with future cases.

These findings may help veterinary teams identify similar cases and better understand how particular FBN1 variants affect cats. They also demonstrate the value of bringing clinicians, genetic researchers, and pet parents together when a case doesn't fit neatly into an existing diagnosis.

Gary and Shaggy's shared genetic variant offered researchers a valuable opportunity to investigate the relationship between their physical features and the underlying condition.

Their owner, Nicole Desmond, also contributed to this process, and Cornell has highlighted the case as an example of how pet parents can collaborate with veterinary and genetic experts to advance knowledge that may eventually benefit other animals.

Even more importantly, Nicole loved the unique feline brothers with her whole heart. Vets did not expect either cat to survive for long, but they defied the odds. Gary was 6 years old when he passed away in July 2024, and in November 2025, at the incredible age of 7, Shaggy joined his brother across the rainbow bridge.

And that's one of the interesting things about veterinary medicine. Not every discovery starts with a large clinical trial or a disease affecting thousands of patients. Sometimes, it begins with two unusual kittens and a veterinary team willing to keep asking questions.

The rarity of this case means we donât necessarily have to think the worst when we see a long-legged kitten; itâs far more likely that theyâre simply long-limbed and not harboring a rare genetic disorder. However, it reminds us to pay attention to the bigger picture, bring unusual findings to the veterinarian's attention, and not automatically assume that two seemingly unrelated problems have nothing to do with each other.

Sometimes, a strange-looking kitten is simply a strange-looking kitten.

And sometimes, those extra-long legs are the first clue to a genetic story that researchers have never documented in cats before.

These festive houseplants bring color, fragrance and greenery to your home long after the decorations come down...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Christmas tree might be the star of the living room in December, but once the holidays are over, it usually gets packed away or recycled. Festive houseplants, on the other hand? Well, they can stick around for years – and some might become so beloved that you can't imagine your home without them.

Whether you're looking to make your Christmas décor a little more lasting, or simply a self-confessed crazy plant lady in need of more houseplants (I'm right there with you!), then you should absolutely consider choosing a living plant this year.

From spectacular seasonal blooms to fragrant herbs and miniature trees, these five festive favorites offer plenty of reasons to keep growing long after the last present has been unwrapped.

I'm a huge fan of Christmas cactus, having inherited one that lived for an incredible 27 years before recently dying. (RIP, Noel; we barely knew ye!) It was a reminder of just how long these festive houseplants can last, and how attached we can become to them over time.

Christmas cactus (Schlumbergera) produces beautiful flowers in shades of pink, red, purple and white, usually just in time for the holidays. Even when it's not in bloom, though, its arching stems make an attractive display, particularly in a hanging pot.

Give it bright indirect light, keep it away from harsh sunshine and don't let its roots sit in soggy compost (mine loved life on our bathroom windowsill), and remember: a cooler spell and shorter days in fall help encourage flowering.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Few festive houseplants make quite as dramatic a statement as amaryllis (Hippeastrum). Its tall stems and oversized trumpet-shaped flowers bring a splash of color indoors when much of the garden is dormant, making it a favorite for Christmas displays.

Somehow, I have managed to keep my own diva alive for several years now (it's sitting on my desk as I type this, in fact), so I urge you not to discard the bulb once flowering finishes. Instead, remove the faded flowers, keep the leaves growing, give it light, water and occasional feeding as it grows, then follow a suitable resting period to encourage another round of blooms. With a little patience, the same bulb can reward you with flowers for many seasons.

You can pick up a bag of Amaryllis bulbs easily enough from the Garden State Bulb Store, if you fancy giving it a go; they'd make excellent holiday presents once you've gotten them started!

If you'd prefer something compact and relatively easy to care for, Flaming Katy (Kalanchoe blossfeldiana) is a solid choice. This succulent produces clusters of bright flowers in red, pink, orange, yellow or white, and it's widely available during the festive season.

Its fleshy leaves store water, so it doesn't need constant watering (making it ideal for even the most forgetful plant parents everywhere). All you have to do is place it somewhere bright, allow the compost to dry a little between drinks, and avoid leaving it sitting in water.

Blooming in the fall and winter, what could be prettier than this Flaming Katy at Christmas?

Flaming Katy can be encouraged to flower again by providing a steady stint of uninterrupted nights in autumn, making it a holiday plant that's well worth keeping after its first colorful display.

Rosemary is a lovely way to bring fragrance into the home over the holidays, especially when sold clipped into a miniature living Christmas tree shape. Its evergreen needles look festive, while its scent adds a little something extra to the season – and you can snip sprigs for cooking, too.

I have actually kept my own rosemary going for a long time, bringing it in and out of the house with the seasons until it grew so large that it eventually had to move permanently into the garden. It just goes to show that a small festive plant can have quite a future ahead of it!

Rosemary (even one like this Rosemary Christmas Tree from the Three Company Store) needs plenty of light and well-drained compost. Don't overwater it, and remember that it generally prefers cooler and brighter conditions than a hot room right next to a radiator.

For something a little different, why not choose a small tree? Fig, olive and citrus trees can all make beautiful container plants, bringing Mediterranean charm to a bright home.

A fig tree offers attractive foliage and the possibility of homegrown fruit, while an olive tree has silvery-green leaves and a timeless look. And there's no denying that a calamondin or miniature orange tree is particularly festive, with glossy foliage, fragrant flowers and colorful fruit that can linger on the branches.

Naturally, these trees need the brightest spot you can offer, and citrus in particular appreciates warmth and consistent care. Indoor conditions aren't always ideal year-round, so check each tree's needs and consider moving it outdoors during suitable warmer months.

A living Christmas plant is a gift that doesn't have to end when the festivities do. Choose yourself, then, a festive houseplant that suits your space, give it the care it needs, and you could be enjoying your festive favorite for many Christmases to come.

Or, you know, you could ask Santa to bring you one. Either or...

#7764. When Art Meets Animal Rescue: A Creative Way to Help Dogs Find Homes

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

We often turn to art for pleasure, curiosity, or a feeling we canât quite put into words. A painting catches our attention; a sculpture makes us pause. But art inspiring us to adopt a dog? Now thereâs a plot twist.

The Rescue Collection is an exciting project created through a collaboration between The Sato Project, creative agencies BLKJ Havas Singapore and Havas New York, and Brooklynâs Powerhouse Arts. The program brings adoptable dogs into the art gallery and uses observations of their responses to create individual artistic profiles. The aim is to help potential adopters see the dogs beyond their appearance, breed, or uncertain past.

Itâs an unusual approach to a familiar challenge: helping rescue dogs get noticed in a crowded adoption landscape.

At Powerhouse Arts in Brooklyn, animal welfare scientist Dr. Holly Molinaro observed dogs from The Sato Project as they explored different artworks. The dogs first had time to sniff around and become comfortable in the unfamiliar space. Their responses were then observed, including whether they looked at, sniffed, or moved away from particular pieces, or chose to lie down nearby.

Rudolph, for example, chose to lie down in front of some sculptures but ignored others. These observations helped shape profiles associating the dogs with artistic styles such as Surrealism, Minimalism, Figurative art, and Abstraction.

The concept is playful, but its purpose is practical. A standard adoption photograph may show what a dog looks like; a creative profile offers another reason to stop scrolling and learn more about the animal behind the image.

Someone might come for the art and leave wanting a dog. Turns out, the best thing in the gallery might have four legs and be up for adoption.

The Sato Project rescues dogs in Puerto Rico and helps place them in homes, including in the northeastern United States. Some arrive with limited information about their histories, and assumptions about a dogâs background can influence how potential adopters perceive them.

A dogâs history can help rescue teams understand what support an animal may need and how to approach introductions to a new home. But the past doesnât tell the whole story. A complicated backstory might tell us where a dog has been. It doesnât tell us everything about who they are. Dogs, much like people, are so much more than their basic profile.

Dogs respond to the world as individuals. One may eagerly approach a stranger, while another prefers to observe from a safe distance. Neither reaction alone defines the dogâs personality or tells us what kind of companion they might become with time and appropriate support.

The Rescue Collection offers a different starting point. Instead of focusing on what is known about a dogâs past, it invites people to become curious about the dog in front of them. That first spark of interest can matter, especially for dogs who might otherwise be overlooked.

Dogs explore their surroundings through several senses, and their behavior around unfamiliar objects can offer clues about what attracts their attention. But interpreting those responses requires care.

Dogs also see color differently from humans. People typically have three types of color-sensitive cone cells in their retinas, while dogs have two, a form of vision known as dichromacy. Dogs distinguish blues and yellows relatively well but have more difficulty differentiating reds and greens. Their visual experience of the world is therefore different from ours.

That doesnât mean dogs see the world in black and white. Color is only one possible influence on how they respond to an object. Shape, contrast, texture, scent, movement, and the surrounding environment may also play a part.

Nor does spending longer near a sculpture necessarily mean a dog prefers its artistic style. The dog may be interested in its shape or position, or simply feel comfortable resting there.

A single gallery visit cannot establish an animalâs overall personality or predict how they will behave around children, other dogs, or visitors at home. Behavior is best understood across time and situations.

A sculpture might have us admiring its color and form. The dog? They might be more interested in giving it a sniff. Different critics, different criteria.

Although the profiles are not scientific personality assessments or guarantees of compatibility, they do invite us to learn more about each dog. Conversations with the rescue team and time spent meeting the dog remain essential to finding a suitable match.

Rescue work involves far more than finding adopters. Veterinary care, foster placements, transportation, behavioral support, and follow-up all require time and resources. Helping the public connect with the dogs is only one part of that work, but an important one.

The Sato Projectâs adoption and foster manager, Alessandra Migliore, said the organization was excited to explore new ways of showcasing its dogsâ personalities. The campaign is part of the organizationâs broader work to help dogs rescued in Puerto Rico find homes in the northeastern United States.

A creative campaign cannot guarantee adoption, and an appealing profile is only the beginning. But an unexpected introduction may reach someone who wasnât actively looking for a dog, or encourage a prospective adopter to look beyond their first impressions.

The Rescue Collection hopes to help more rescue dogs connect with potential adopters. Its message says it best: âSee the masterpiece inside every dog.â

Art might catch someoneâs eye, but getting to know the dog is what matters. And if a sculpture-loving visitor leaves the gallery thinking about adoption, thatâs a pretty good review.

Explore The Rescue Collection, use its rescue-finding tool to search by city or postcode, or meet dogs waiting for homes through The Sato Project.

#7763. How to Create a Temporary Workshop Anywhere

Black Friday Deals Are Already Here ➡️ Tools, Generators, Essentials & More

Published Nov 23, 2026 3:46 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Doing home projects out in a garage or down in a basement workshop isn’t always possible. And even when it is possible, it’s not always the best option, especially if you need to carry heavy, oversized, or delicate materials throughout your home. Instead, it’s sometimes better to set up a temporary workshop where you need to work.

After years spent as a construction project manager moving my tools and materials between warehouses, work sites, and the homes/businesses of our customers, I developed an easy system for setting up a quick and effective temporary workshop with just a few key components. Keep reading to find out exactly what you need to create your own temporary workshop at your home.

Working on the floor strains your back, while working on dining tables risks costly dents and scratches. Instead, it’s always good to have a portable workbench that’s easy to set up and take down, like the Keter Folding Workbench. A stable and reliable surface makes projects more efficient, since you won’t need to be bending over to cut, glue, or drill.

Additionally, the workbench can act as a simple support when you need to measure materials, set up a miter saw, or clamp your materials so that they don’t shift while you work. If you don’t want to purchase or build a new workbench for this purpose, you can also set up a pair of heavy-duty collapsible sawhorses paired with a sacrificial plywood sheet to give you a waist-high surface that folds flat for storage.

Floor and countertop protection prevents permanent damage and can reduce your cleanup time by half. For this reason, it’s essential to plan for surface protection and cleanup when you are setting up your temporary workshop.

Drape moving blankets or thick canvas drop cloths over tables, counters, or hardwood floors to absorb impacts and catch dropped tools. Unlike plastic tarps, heavy canvas stays put and prevents items from sliding around. To help keep your temporary workshop clean and organized, include a small wet/dry shop vac fitted with a disposable fleece filter bag to capture messes at the source so you can pack up in minutes.

Treated with a special coating, this heavy-duty tarp repels moisture in addition to offering protection to your work surface. Learn more.

Without a heavy, bolted-down bench vise, clamps act as your third hand to hold materials steady while cutting, gluing, or drilling. Keep two or three medium-sized bar clamps handy to secure materials directly to a table edge or sawhorse. These clamps are often easy to store when not in use, so they won’t get in the way while you work.

Also, you can lay a rubberized mesh pad, like this POWERTEC Nonslip Mat, under smaller pieces when sanding or routing. It holds flat workpieces steady using friction alone, leaving the entire top surface unobstructed.

Overhead room lighting casts shadows right over your hands when you lean over a project to see what you are doing, increasing mistakes and safety risks. But holding a flashlight while you work just ties up one of your hands, severely limiting your control and efficiency. Instead, it’s better to find task lights that are made for versatility so you can focus on the project, rather than fighting with dim lighting.

A directional light clipped to a shelf, chair, or table edge lets you aim bright light directly at your cut line or assembly area. Opt for a high-lumen LED clamp light or magnetic work light to illuminate your temporary workshop, like this ZONE LED Clamp Work Light.

Indoor outlets are often far from where you need to work and rarely have enough open receptacles. A 12-gauge, multi-outlet cord with built-in GFCI protection, such as this CCCEI Extension Cord, safely handles high-draw power tools while protecting you from electrical faults. It can also be used to power a space heater for a temporary cold weather workshop upgrade if you need to work outside or in an uninsulated space.

Use a thick-gauge cord to safely run high-draw power tools from a wall outlet to your temporary station without overheating or losing power. Additionally, use a surge-protected power strip with wide-spaced outlets for your battery chargers, task lights, and smaller tools. Wide spacing prevents bulky power bricks from blocking adjacent plugs.

After months of scouring the market and putting products through their paces, we’ve named the best of the best in new tools. There’s something for everyone, from veteran pros to average Joes.

#7762. John Yoo on "Leaving a [University of] California that Rejects the West"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Professor John Yoo explains his decision to leave the University of California at Berkeley

Professor John Yoo is leaving the law school at the University of California at Berkeley to join the School of Civic Leadership at the University of Texas at Austin. As I noted here, his departure means there will not be a single right-leaning professor teaching public law subjects at Berkeley--and no more than a handful (if that) at all of the UC schools combined.

Given the attention his move has received, Yoo has written an op-ed for the New York Post explaining his decision to choose Texas, and disputing any suggestion that he was driven out of Berkeley.

I'm leaving not because I feel driven out by Berkeley — anything but.

In my three decades there I've enjoyed working, on an individual level, with spirited, ambitious students and challenging, innovative scholars.

I'm moving because Berkeley, like its peers, has declined from a daring, risk-taking center of higher learning to one that wallows contentedly in a monoculture of liberalism.

Yoo says the school has been obsessed with ethnic diversity while disregarding viewpoint diversity, and that this has eroded the institution's commitment to free speech and created an environment in which anti-semitism has taken root.

I've watched students and the usual agitators disrupt debates on affirmative action, spark pitched fights on Sproul Plaza and try to shout down distinguished scholars and thinkers (home of the Free Speech Movement, indeed).

Tolerance of such shenanigans was matched by intolerance of conservative or libertarian views on the faculty.

Berkeley has consistently rejected conservative scholars, no matter how well-qualified, well-published or widely cited. . . .

One famous member of a revered Berkeley humanities department (always ranked among the nation's top three) once told me directly that he would never hire a conservative. . . .

Most student groups at Berkeley Law now boycott any event with a speaker who believes in Israel's right to exist.

For the first time in my 33 years at Berkeley I witnessed a heckler's veto, as protesters prevented a member of the Israeli Knesset from speaking — and top university officials stood idly by.

Students posted flyers depicting the dean of the law school — a liberal scholar with whom I rarely agree — feasting on human beings, then physically invaded his home while he hosted members of the graduating class, simply because he is Jewish.

Yoo argues that great universities should refocus their teaching on Western Civilization, so that the nation does not lose sight of the ideals upon which it was founded and the principles that provide the foundation for western prosperity.

The emergence of human reason in Greece and religious revelation in Jerusalem produced the free markets, natural rights, rule of law and democratic self-government that have made our astounding prosperity and power possible.

These ideals run directly counter to the poison running rampant on our campuses. . . .

Texas wants to restore Western civilization and the great books to the center of its curriculum — not to blindly agree with the past, but to understand and debate it.

I'm eager to join the Texans who want to defend free speech and thought, and to leave behind a California that rejects the West.

#7761. Paws and Effect: The Reasons Behind a Cat’s Sudden Aggression

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

We all know that feline behavior can be somewhat unpredictable. Just when you think youâve got it all figured out, a cat is already three steps ahead of you. But thereâs a big difference between normal feline quirks and uncharacteristic aggression.

A cat that has always been gentle and suddenly starts lashing out may be reacting to something in its environment, changing hormones, pain, or a health problem. Aggression has many causes, from fear and frustration to competition with other cats. Understanding what has changed can help identify the cause and determine the best way to respond.

Unneutered male cats may fight over access to females, particularly when several cats are competing for mates in the same area. When a female cat is in heat, she may attract multiple males, making fights more likely.

Female cats can also behave differently during heat cycles. Many become unusually affectionate and demanding of attention, while others may become irritable or aggressive. Hormonal changes can also affect how they interact with other cats, particularly other females.

Spaying/neutering is an important aspect of taking care of a cat. Not only does it help to minimize aggression and friction between cats, but it also prevents unwanted litters and helps reduce the risk of certain diseases.

Pain can make even a normally friendly cat lash out. A cat may react aggressively if someone touches a sore area or approaches when it is feeling unwell.

Urinary tract disease can make a cat pretty miserable, and males in particular are vulnerable to urinary blockages, which are extremely painful and can become life-threatening. A cat that is straining to urinate or unable to pass urine needs emergency veterinary attention.

Infections, injuries, arthritis, and cancer are often painful but difficult to recognize from the outside. If aggression appears suddenly or seems linked to discomfort, a veterinary examination is an important first step.

A frightened cat may respond aggressively when startled, even if it is usually relaxed and friendly. A sudden noise, an unfamiliar person, or another threatening experience can trigger a defensive reaction.

Ongoing stress can also contribute to aggression. Cats that feel unsafe in their surroundings may remain on edge and react defensively to people or animals around them.

Every cat should have access to a quiet, comfortable place where it can retreat without being disturbed. Giving a frightened cat space can help it feel more secure.

Not every aggressive-looking interaction is driven by anger or fear. Play helps cats practise their hunting skills, and some become too rough when playing with people or other animals.

However, rough play should not be encouraged because biting and scratching can cause injuries. Rewarding gentle play and redirecting a cat toward appropriate toys can help it learn more acceptable ways to use its energy.

Cats can be protective of their territory, so the arrival of another animal may trigger aggression. The newcomer could be a new cat or dog in the household, or an outdoor cat that has started visiting the yard.

Sometimes, owners may not even realize another cat is nearby. Seeing or smelling an unfamiliar animal can leave a cat agitated, causing it to react to other pets or people.

Aggressive behavior plus inappropriate urination and scent-marking are not uncommon when a cat feels its territory is under threat.

A cat that becomes frustrated by something it cannot reach may take that frustration out on another target. This is known as redirected aggression.

For example, a cat might become agitated after seeing another cat outside, then lash out at a person or pet nearby. The target may have done nothing wrong and simply been in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Giving an agitated cat time and space to calm down is safer than trying to handle it immediately.

Cats living together usually have established social relationships, and introducing a new pet tends to upset the status quo. A certain amount of fighting and posturing is to be expected as the cats adjust to the change, but escalating aggression or bullying of one cat should be addressed.

Introducing a new animal gradually can help reduce conflict. Cats should have time to become familiar with each other without being forced into close contact before they are ready.

Some cats seem to enjoy attention but suddenly bite or scratch once petting begins. A cat may become overstimulated by touch, or it may simply want to be near a person without being handled.

Watch for signs of discomfort, such as flattened ears or a flicking tail. If a cat seems agitated, stop petting and give it space. Treats can reward calm interactions when the cat is comfortable.

Aggression can be difficult for a household to manage, but many causes can be addressed with patience and the right approach. Rewarding calm behavior, avoiding known triggers, and providing a safe place to retreat can all help.

The first step is to work out why the cat is behaving differently. If the aggression is sudden, it may be linked to pain or illness, so you should always consult a veterinarian before treating it as a behavioral issue. Once medical causes are excluded, look for changes â both indoors and outside the home â that might be affecting your cat.

Simple steps like providing extra hiding places, calming aids, and adapting handling techniques can go a long way to reducing feline aggression.

I remember when my mom brought home our first fosters. I was in fifth grade, and when my twin sister, Becca, and I came home from school, our mom walked us over to a box with three little neonatal kittens, just days old: Amelia, Angel, and Buddy. With closed eyes and little bodies running purely on instinct, they wriggled over one another, crying out to be fed. I watched as my mom gently picked them up, and as she did, she turned to us, smiling, and said, âtheyâre your responsibilityâ.

I was flooded with excitement and fear all at once. I knew nothing about caring for something so small. I watched in awe as my mom bottle-fed them one by one. The meowing subsided, and their little ears wiggled as they latched on and ate until their tiny bellies were full. The lesson had begun regardless of my fears. But feeding, I quickly learned, was just step one.

Soon after, we were stimulating each kitten to go potty, testing the temperature of their enclosure, wiping them clean, and getting them settled in for a post-bottle nap. So much happened so quickly, and they were so small and fragile. I told my mom I was nervous that I wouldnât be able to do what she did. She laughed and, with a grin, informed me I would have plenty of time to learn: Amelia, Angel, and Buddy would need to eat every 2 hours, even throughout the night. So we had lots of chances to practice and retain all the new skills she was showing us.

Over the next few weeks, we watched them grow and grow until they were ready to find their forever homes. As adoption day approached, it was incredibly hard. My sister and I begged our mom to let us keep the kittens. After all, we had raised them, and our love for them was undeniable. But she assured us that this was a good thing; letting them go meant we could help more animals in need. In the moment, however, I didnât understand. Instead, I cried myself to sleep holding the kittens. My kittens.

Then the day came, and even though the adopters were my friends, I bristled when they knocked at the door. But as they came in and met Amelia, Angel and Buddy, something magical happened: I watched my friends fall in love with them just like I had. They giggled at the clumsy way Buddy walked. Their hearts melted as they watched the girls cuddle in the sun. I was still scared to let the kittens go, but now part of me was excited, too. My friends saw them how I saw them. I had to trust that the little babies that we raised were on to bigger and better things. Things that would allow us to welcome another baby in need. But still, my heart broke - I had fallen in love with each of them, and saying goodbye terrified me.

There wasnât much time after they were adopted to worry about my fears, though. Before I knew it, we said hello to our next foster: a skittish and energetic 5-week-old boy we called Kipper. I thought maybe this time Iâd try to guard my heart, but Kipper stole it anyway. His silly antics and never-ending supply of energy made it impossible not to fall in love with him, too. Part of me hoped that maybe this time, Kipper could stay. But my mom held firm, and a few weeks later another friend came to us to adopt. I watched it play out all over again. I smiled as they swooned over this little precious kitten and all his quirks, just like I had.

This time, though I was still heartbroken, I felt a sense of understanding settle in, too. I remember thinking to myself, as Kipper fell asleep, purring, in my friendâs arms, âI wonder who we will get to help next?â

It didnât take long for that question to get its answer: Four tiny black-and-white kittens found in a hot tub and brought to our doorstep. Three were friendly; one, wellâ¦he was anything but! Cleo, Leo, and Brandy settled in beautifully, but Bindy just needed more.

More time, more attention, more understanding.

I felt drawn to him, and while my twin tended to the others, I found myself focused on Bindy. He would hide, hiss, spit, and bite. But really, he was just a little thing in a big world, and he was terrified. I worked with him every day, and slowly but surely, he made progress. When adoption day came around, however, we decided Bindy wasnât ready yet. He stayed behind to gain more confidence and, in time, became our first foster-fail.

Sometimes it was best for a foster to be adopted, but sometimes, they were already home.

Bindy eventually became the most loving cat I ever knew. He was my soul cat, and my best friend. And even though he stayed, I didnât avoid the heartbreak that came with saying goodbye; it just came many, many years later when old age finally took him. I learned a second lesson from Bindy then: there is no love without loss and, despite the pain, love would always be worth it.

So I continued to dive in, foster after foster. Heartbreak after heartbreak. Miracle after miracle. And it was always worth it; just like my mom said it would be. Iâm no longer the little girl learning from my mother; those lessons are now a part of me. Theyâre one of the things she left behind after a lifetime of love. My heart broke saying goodbye to her, too, but her teachings gave me a life thatâs filled to the brim with purpose. And paired with a passion inspired by my first foster fail, Bindy, I quickly developed a soft spot for the âspicyâ foster cats; and thatâs what I do now.

Currently, a euthanasia-list survivor is calling my home their safe haven. Just like Bindy, Simon wasterrified and aggressive, and he almost paid for it with his life. While Iâve been fostering him, however, Iâve gotten to know a completely different cat than the one in the shelter. A cat thatâs full of love and silly antics, whoâs eager to hold a conversation and meow for your attention. A cat who just needed a chance.

When his adoption day comes, I know my heart will break again; it always does. Itâs the price we pay for loving something, and Iâll pay that price over and over again because it means I get to watch someone adore him in all the ways I have, and more. The internet will go into an uproar demanding I keep him, but my momâs voice will sound clearly in my ear and keep me grounded:

âItâs a good thing. Letting them go means we can help others in need.â

So I'll say goodbye, knowing another Simon, Bindy, or Kipper is waiting for their chance to be loved. And as I walk back into the shelter, the lesson I began learning all those years ago in fifth grade remains true: Fostering Saves Lives.

Old-style holiday bulbs that run hot can help reduce the chill for potted plants on a frosty night. But there are a few details to get right before you try it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every November, boxes of holiday lights come down from the attic, and a few gardeners start eyeing those tangled strands for a second job. On paper, Christmas lights frost protection sounds like a neighbor's tip over coffee – string up a potted lemon tree, plug it in, and hope it makes it to morning.

There's some truth to it. Gardeners have relied on heat from old-style bulbs for years, and it can work alongside the usual steps for winterizing container plants, like covering pots or moving them under shelter. When used safely with a suitable cover or enclosure, that heat can nudge the temperature around a plant up a few degrees.

The catch is that only certain bulbs produce enough heat to help, and most modern porch strands won't help at all. But using the right bulbs comes with its own risks. Mix hot bulbs, fabric covers, and unprotected electrical connections outdoors carelessly, and you have a fire and shock hazard.

Christmas lights keep plants warm only if the bulbs run hot. Old-fashioned incandescent bulbs, like these C7 Christmas lights from Amazon, give off a fair amount of heat along with their light, so running a strand beneath a properly supported frost cover or inside a cold frame can warm the small area around a plant. University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources advises home citrus growers to use traditional non-LED lights to provide extra warmth, with or without a frost blanket.

Colorado State University Extension measured the effect in cold frame trials in Fort Collins. One string of 25 mid-size C7 bulbs hung inside a covered cold frame, with a space blanket over the frame, kept each frame noticeably warmer than the night outside. A string also beat a single large bulb at warming the cold corners.

If you want to recreate an enclosed space like that, use a cold frame or mini greenhouse, but only if the structure allows the lights to be safely suspended away from the plants and covering.

Pick up a string of Christmas lights in a store today, and you'll likely find they're LEDs. They convert far more of their electricity into light, leaving little heat behind – fine for decoration but useless for shielding a citrus tree on a 28°F (-2°C) night. When it comes to LED lights, frost protection just isn't on the table – they don't generate enough warmth.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

University frost guidelines specifically recommend incandescent bulbs when you need real heat. Traditional incandescent mini lights can provide some warmth, while larger C7 and C9 bulbs, like these from Novelty Lights Store, produce more heat per bulb.

Any set used should carry an outdoor rating and be suitable for the intended setup. With incandescent Christmas lights, plants under a properly supported cover can gain extra heat, but the same heat makes the bulbs a hazard if they touch foliage or covering materials.

Several vulnerable container plants could benefit, but growers most often protect potted citrus this way. Cold damage can begin around 30°F (-1°C), depending on the variety and duration of exposure, with limes generally more sensitive than mandarins. A potted lemon on the patio faces a specific risk that an in-ground tree doesn't. Its roots are far less cold-hardy than its branches, and the small amount of potting mix around them can cool and freeze much faster than the soil around an in-ground tree.

That means the lights can help through brief cold spells – just a few nights with light frost. They're not enough to protect tropical plants during weeks of hard freezes. A larger container holds more potting mix and can provide some extra insulation for the roots, so a pot like the ModernNest fiberstone planter from Walmart, designed to withstand freezing conditions, gives a citrus tree a sturdier home but won't prevent its roots from freezing.

Hot incandescent bulbs can cause damage if they come into contact with foliage or covering materials. Incandescent bulbs can burn leaves if they touch them directly. Frost cloth, sheets, plastic wrap, and space blankets should never be pressed against the lights, where they can scorch, melt, or become a fire risk. Hang the strand so each bulb has enough clearance from surrounding materials, and use a separate frame, stakes, or supports to keep covers up and away from the bulbs. Make sure the lights are securely positioned so they cannot shift into contact with the covering.

Water and electricity can create hazards on cold nights. Use only outdoor-rated lights and cords outside, and plug them into a GFCI-protected outlet. Throw out any strand with cracked sockets or frayed wire instead of hanging it. Keep indoor strands and household power strips indoors, and don't rely on tape to waterproof electrical connections. Follow the manufacturer's limits on how many strings can be connected end to end, and follow the safety instructions packed with the product.

Start by moving the pot. An unheated garage, shed, or closed-in porch that stays above freezing can carry a citrus tree through a cold snap with no wiring. Pots that stay outside belong together, up against a house wall or in a corner out of the wind. Water them well before the cold comes, since moist potting mix freezes more slowly than dry.

Covers and wraps add another layer. Lowe's sells a 2-ounce frost blanket that can go over the plant on cold nights and come off during the day. Around the container, slip on an Eonox drawstring pot insulation cover to keep cold wind off the root zone.

For plants that need steady heat for weeks, a thermostatically controlled heater inside a greenhouse built to house one is the safer setup – the Dr Infrared greenhouse heater has an adjustable thermostat.

Under a cover or in a cold frame, old incandescent holiday lights can add a few degrees, maybe enough to see potted citrus through a short, light frost. You can't count on them, though, and the method needs careful setup, even though it's recommended by several university extension services. An LED strand won't give a cold plant any real protection.

Using hot bulbs with fabric and outdoor power for improvised heating carries risks that are easy to underestimate. Proper shelter, insulation, and a good frost blanket are generally safer options, although they won't always provide as much warmth as a safely heated enclosure.

For most gardeners, the simplest solution is to keep the twinkling lights on the porch this year and move your lemon tree into a frost-free garage when cold weather hits. It'll still be green when the holiday decorations go back in the attic.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7757. Is That Really A Service Dog?

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

For years, business owners and property managers have wrestled with the same question: how do you tell the difference between a legitimate service animal and a pet that someone is trying to pass off as one?

Itâs a question John Bradford spent years trying to answer, first as a property manager overseeing thousands of rental units, and now as the founder of PetScreening, a platform used to verify animal accommodation requests across more than 7 million rental units nationwide.

With the rising number of service dogs and emotional support animals leading to incidents of confusion, conflict, and exploitation, John sets the record straight on how to verify a real service animal from one that isn't, and what you are legally allowed to ask.

The truth is that most people donât fully understand the laws around service animals and emotional support animals, and even well-meaning questions can come across as anything but. That gray area and confusion can create real risk. Ask the wrong question, and a business can face a discrimination complaint. Ask no questions at all, and policies and rules become easy to bend, which leads to potentially dangerous situations.

Getting this right protects everyone involved, including the people who genuinely rely on these animals every day.

Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), service animals are defined as:

âDogs that are individually trained to do work or perform tasks for people with disabilities.â

Disabilities vary widely, from physical and sensory to psychiatric, intellectual, and neurological. The needs of each person are different, so the trained tasks may look different from person to person.  The ADA cites that the service animal must be a dog or, in rare cases, a miniature horse. Federal law does not require certifications, registrations, vests, or ID cards for these animals.

Beyond the specification that the animal must be trained to perform tasks, the legal standard is limited, so it can be difficult to easily identify which animals are legitimately service dogs and which are not. This is where public confusion starts.

There are plenty of ways to make a dog look like a service animal, like labeled vests, âregistrationâ certifications, and IDs, but none of these are federally supported. A dog wearing a vest isnât automatically a service animal, and a dog without one isnât automatically a pet. What matters legally is not appearance or paperwork. Itâs the dogâs trained ability to perform certain tasks.

This is the distinction many find hardest to grasp, and it matters because different laws apply to each. Service dogs are protected under the ADA and, due to their training and the tasks they perform, they are permitted in public spaces such as restaurants, retail stores, and hotels. That could mean guiding someone who is visually impaired, alerting an owner to an oncoming seizure, or reminding them to take medication. Service animals are also protected under the Fair Housing Act and require paperwork if the disability or need for the animal is not obviously understood.

Emotional support animals (ESAs) are different. Their value comes from the comfort their presence provides. They donât necessarily have to be dogs, they arenât required to be trained to perform specific tasks, and theyâre not covered by the ADA to be allowed in public spaces like restaurants.

They are, however, protected by the Fair Housing Act. Under this, landlords are generally required to make allowances for an ESA if a tenant has appropriate documentation from a licensed healthcare provider establishing a disability-related need. Examples of disabilities warranting an ESA include, but are not limited to, anxiety disorders or autism.

ESA accommodations are supposed to come through legitimate means, typically an established relationship with a licensed medical or mental health professional who can document the need. But some people have found loopholes for this by filling out forms online or paying fees for instant letters, which only fuels public skepticism about the legitimate need for these animals. Not to mention, this abuse can make people wary of service dogs, too.

While there is no foolproof visual test, trained service animals typically display consistent, recognizable behaviors. These dogs show exemplary discipline and obedience to the commands of their handler. They have the ability to ignore external distractions from other dogs, people, food, sounds, and smells while focusing on the needs of their handler. They display a calm temperament and are not aggressive or anxious. It is also expected that these animals be quiet, unless they are tasked with alerting an owner to a medical issue, and that they are housebroken and trained to walk on a leash without unnecessary pulling or circling.

This is where business owners and landlords need to tread carefully. When it isnât obvious that a dog is a service animal, staff are permitted to ask:

Is this dog required because of a disability?

What task has it been trained to perform?

Thatâs the full extent of it. Staff should not ask about the nature of a personâs disability, demand documentation or proof of training, or require dogs to demonstrate their tasks. Asking beyond the two questions, even if it comes from a place of genuine curiosity or caution, can expose a business to discrimination claims.

News stories about supposed service animals harming bystanders in public continue to raise questions about the legitimacy of those animals, and businesses are often caught in the crossfire. These incidents are symptoms of a larger problem: businesses and property owners navigating without clear guidance, while people with legitimate needs are met with suspicion.

Service animals and emotional support animals play an essential role in the lives of the people who rely on them, and protecting that role starts with understanding the rules.

If you own a business or manage a property, you donât need to become legal experts overnight, but you do need a consistent, fair process that respects peopleâs rights and keeps everyone safe. When everyone knows where the lines are, the people who truly depend on these animals can go about their lives without facing doubt at every door.

As a cat parent, youâll no doubt be aware that living with cats is a completely different game than owning other pets. But did you know that this isnât just a matter of perception?

Cats have only been domesticated for about half as long as dogs have. On top of that, their genes are much less susceptible to âshapingâ than those of dogs. The result? Cats have retained more wild feline physical traits, instincts, and tendencies than dogs.

Not only does this have a significant impact on feline behavior, but it also shapes how we care for them.

This fact has been the driving force behind Petlibro's approach to high-tech cat care products. From pet fountains and automatic feeders to self-cleaning litter boxes, this company understands cats and knows exactly what they need to stay healthy and happy.

Here, we take a closer look at five of their productsâeach designed for your catâs specific needs while making your life easier.

Cats are complex creatures, and it takes more than love, cuddles, and the occasional tasty treat to keep them truly engaged, enriched, and thriving. In fact, they often need more than what the average owner can provide with their own two hands.

I could go on all day about the importance of a high-quality diet for your cat. But today, I want to talk about an aspect of the feline diet most owners might not think about: the importance of small, consistent, proportioned meals.

Cats evolved as hunters of relatively small prey, so their natural feeding pattern is quite different from ours and from the typical pet dog.

A wild cat might spend much of its day moving through its territory, hunting, and eating multiple small meals when the opportunity presents itself. They are not accustomed to sitting down to one or two large meals each day.

Although the process of domestication means that your feline family member no longer needs to hunt down their next meal, those instincts haven't completely disappeared just because their food comes in a bowl.

Even more so than eating habits, drinking habits in cats are highly tied to their instincts and physiological needs.

Domestic cats evolved from desert wild cats. That arid climate impacted their relationship to water in two key ways:

First, desert wild cats evolved to get most of their water from their preyâwhich isnât much. This means their kidneys are highly specialized to retain water and pass very little of it through their urine. For a cat that eats several juicy mice each day, this is all well and good. For a pet cat eating dry food, the need to consume water is dramatically increased if they are to keep this super-efficient system running properly. However, the instinct to actively seek out drinking water has not entirely caught up with the domesticated catâs lifestyle.

This brings us to cat hydration key number two: Desert wild cats know better than to drink stagnant water. In hot, arid climates, still water breeds bacteria and other dangerous organisms. As a result, cats are naturally attracted to fresh, flowing water that is much safer to drink; something that remains true for our pets.

Your kitty may be a skilled hunter and the apex predator of your home, but, like their wildcat ancestors, they can also be prey animals, with instincts that evolved to evade larger predators. One place this becomes evident is in their bathroom habits.

Cats bury their urine and feces to hide the scent from potential predators and competitors, so a stinky litter box feels anything but safe. And if they donât feel safe there, they may find other places to eliminate waste. Or worse, hold it in, causing kidney and digestive issues.

These three key areas are where Petlibroâs products shine. Created with your catâs natural instincts and needs in mind, they were also designed to make your life easier.

Allowing pets to graze or âfree-feedâ is a major cause of obesity in domestic cats. Because their wild ancestors never knew when their next meal was coming, their instincts tell them to eat whenever food is available. If itâs always available, some cats will simply keep on eating, even if they donât feel hungry.

An automatic feeder does a lot more than make mealtime convenient. It can actually help you create a feeding routine that better suits your cat's instincts, providing several small meals throughout the day, rather than one or two large ones.

From a human perspective, an automatic feeder can also provide that âcrack of dawnâ meal many cats crave, without you having to leave the comfort of your bed!

If your cat seems inexplicably fascinated by the faucet, they may actually be telling you something. Cats instinctively prefer fresh, moving water. By embracing the behavior that helped their wild ancestors survive, a water fountain can help our pets thrive.

The PETLIBRO Dockstream 2 Smart Cordless Fountain taps into that instinct while simultaneously helping you keep track of your cat's hydration.

Its pet-sensing mode activates the flow when your cat approaches, while a four-layer filtration system helps keep water fresh and clean. Just as important, the Petlibro App lets you monitor drinking habits and alerts you to changes in water intake, water levels, filter replacement, and cleaning.

With a cordless design and long battery life, you can give your cat the fresh, flowing water they instinctively seek without needing to keep the fountain tethered to an outlet, meaning you can place the fountain in whichever location your cat prefers.

A self-cleaning litter box isnât just about making our lives easier; itâs about providing your cat with a fresh litter box for every visit, without having to scoop multiple times a day. Cats need a space that is clean, private, and feels safe. That makes keeping the litter box tidy and odor-free an important part of supporting their natural behavior.

The PETLIBRO Luma Smart Automatic Cat Litter Box with Camera ensures a clean, safe bathroom space while turning the litter box into a source of useful information about your cat.

Luma automatically scoops after each visit, keeping the box consistently clean while locking away odors with a built-in carbon deodorizer. But the real high-tech advantage is what happens behind the scenes. The Lumaâs camera and AI software recognize up to ten individual cats and log their litter box visits, while waste analysis can help detect changes in urine and stool. You can even check in through the camera and receive alerts about unusual activity, including increased or decreased use.

In other words, Luma doesnât just help your cat establish a healthy bathroom routine, but it also gives you the data you need to see critical changes in health before they become something more.

The common thread among all of these products is simple: The best technology doesnât try to change what makes cats, cats. It works with them.

By understanding the instincts that still shape how our domesticated companions eat, drink, and eliminate, Petlibro turns everyday cat care into an opportunity to support those natural needs while giving owners more insight and peace of mind.
