#7623. Rule 14a-8: Perhaps Slow-Walking Recission is Best

In a recent post on the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance, titled “Rule 14a-8: Perhaps There’s Another Way,” Sarah Wilson, Founder and CEO of Minerva Analytics, tackles the hot topic of Rule 14a-8 rescission. At bottom, she argues for implementing a version of the UK Takeover Panel to regulate procedural requirements for proposal submission while leaving decisions about content scope to shareholders. Along the way, she argues that The Heritage Foundation, including by way of its American Investor Initiative, “is having second thoughts” about prior positions Heritage has taken on the issue, and that Heritage “seems distinctly unhappy with the SEC’s direction of travel” and is thus left in “the strange position of defending the very mechanism it spent years arguing had made shareholder meetings too political.” These characterizations of Heritage warrant some clarification.

To begin with, we at Heritage certainly hope we never stop assessing past positions in the light of current experience, and that we will always do our best to reflect the latest understanding of the myriad factors impacting policies over time. Having said that, our current view of Rule 14a-8 is not nearly as conflicted as Wilson presents.

For example, Wilson contrasts our past criticism of proxy advisers, ESG and “woke investment,” with our current position of cautioning against too hasty rescission of Rule 14a-8. Specifically, as we noted in a recent letter published in the Wall Street Journal, we believe the goal of depoliticizing corporate governance is best served by a “generous grace period” before rescission takes effect.

The current mix of corporate commitments took shape over decades in which mainly one set of proponents used the proposal process. Proponents who favor corporate neutrality, Heritage among them, have only recently begun to use the process effectively. Ending it abruptly would freeze in place the results of that one-sided period. A transition period would also allow states to develop their own frameworks for shareholder proposals, give companies and investors time to adjust, and avoid entrenching a status quo that formed under proxy-advisory and asset-manager voting practices that are themselves only now being reformed.

While our position may in some sense have shifted from “keep the rule” to “rescind the rule slowly,” the animating principle remains the same: The prosperity-generating power of free-market capitalism must be defended against the myriad conflicts of interest distorting relevant inputs from corporate leaders, asset managers, proxy advisors, activists, and others. Particularly with respect to ESG (including DEI, sustainability, and net zero, as well as the successor labels under which similar commitments are increasingly marketed), resisting the use of corporate and regulatory machinery to advance policy goals that could not be achieved through markets or legislatures is a consistent theme. As has been said: “Every great cause begins as a movement, becomes a business, and eventually degenerates into a racket.”

>>> The Case of the Missing Heritage Foundation Proposals

To illustrate, consider the four justifications most commonly offered for corporate sustainability commitments and investments, and why each, on closer examination, proves incomplete. First, sustainability commitments are often described as a matter of legal compliance. But the leading climate-disclosure mandates, such as California’s SB 253 and SB 261, require companies to report emissions and climate-related risks, not to adopt reduction targets. And when we have offered to withdraw shareholder proposals if a company would state publicly that its sustainability commitments are legally required, companies have generally declined to do so. That reluctance suggests the commitments rest on something other than compliance.

Second, sustainability commitments are frequently defended as risk management, a necessary cost of reducing exposure to climate-related harm. But according to the Global Carbon Budget 2025, the United States accounts for roughly 13 percent of global fossil CO₂ emissions, compared with about 32 percent for China and 8 percent for India. Even if every U.S. corporation reached net zero, the effect on global emissions, and so on the physical risks companies face, would be modest without comparable action elsewhere. Firm-level transition risks, such as regulatory and litigation exposure, may justify some measures. But those risks call for targeted, quantified responses, not open-ended commitments.

Third, sustainability commitments are said to reflect client demand. BlackRock’s 2020 letter to clients, for example, justified its sustainability initiatives in part by noting that “more and more of our clients have focused on the impact of sustainability on their portfolios.” Client demand alone, however, does not show that a commitment creates value for shareholders. Demand for a product does not justify supplying it at any price, and sustainability commitments deserve the same discipline. Their costs and benefits should be fully disclosed so that clients and shareholders can make informed judgments.

Finally, one would expect companies making substantial sustainability commitments to have done the relevant expected-value analysis and to track the returns. Yet even advocates of corporate sustainability acknowledge that this rarely happens. The director of NYU Stern’s Center for Sustainable Business has observed that “most companies are not monetizing the Return on Sustainability Investment,” and that financial benefits “are tracked differently (if at all) by different units and are not aggregated.” Without such measurement, it is difficult to assess whether these commitments serve shareholders’ interests.

If these conventional justifications are incomplete, a further explanation lies in the incentives of the parties involved. Asset managers market ESG products and compete for mandates from clients who want them. Proxy advisors have offered ESG-related advisory services alongside their voting recommendations. And corporate managers benefit from the wide discretion that stakeholder-oriented commitments afford.  Other incentives may reinforce these: avoiding confrontations with activist investors, the reputational benefits of visible sustainability commitments in settings such as the World Economic Forum, the social and professional norms within which many executives and directors operate, and bias against people of faith. Together, these incentives help explain why corporations would adopt net zero commitments without documented support for their returns, despite well-documented concerns about affordability, national security, and energy independence.

>>> More Than Ever, It’s Time for Economic Freedom, Not DEI or ESG

All the foregoing also helps explain low vote counts on anti-ESG proposals. Once you’ve accounted for the influence of conflicted asset managers, proxy advisors, and corporate insiders—and public pension funds whose voting policies may weigh collateral policy objectives alongside beneficiaries’ financial interests—there aren’t many votes left that can reflect the views of the “true owners.” As Jerry Bowyer, also mentioned in Wilson’s article, has essentially noted, if a foreign country’s national election returned 2% or less of the votes in favor of a candidate widely known to only have 50% of the support, all the defenders of democracy would be calling the election corrupt and illegitimate.

Yet this is basically what we see in proxy voting every season when it comes to conservative anti-ESG and anti-DEI proposals. Vote totals can also be misread in the other direction. When an anti-DEI proposal receives 2% support, the result is sometimes reported as showing that 98 percent of shareholders ‘support DEI.’ Yet comparable pro-DEI proposals have recently drawn similarly low support, particularly since asset managers revised their voting policies and proxy advisors came under regulatory scrutiny. That pattern suggests low totals often reflect reluctance to support prescriptive proposals of either kind, not an endorsement of the underlying policy.

All the foregoing helps explain why Heritage believes rescinding Rule 14a-8 too quickly would turn laudable federalism into problematic favoritism by sealing in conflicted gains just when free-market proponents have started making material gains getting corporations back to neutral. And that position can be completely consistent with also supporting the ultimate rescission of the rule due to it being unauthorized and undermining proper federalism.

Much more can, should, and will be said about the proper balance of state oversight of proposal submission and scope requirements, as well as federal oversight of related corporate disclosures in interstate commerce. But for now, it is worth noting that a consistent theme animates Heritage’s past and present positions on Rule 14a-8. Heritage certainly appreciates the ways we are witnessing private ordering, federalism, and the marketplace of ideas operating in response to the proposed rescission of the rule, but we are in fact happy “with the SEC’s direction of travel.”

#7622. Jonathan Scott’s Trick for Making a Fake Christmas Tree Look Real Is Brilliant

Jonathan Scott shares his favorite Christmas decorating tricks, from making artificial trees look real to refreshing decor without spending more.

There’s no place like home for the holidays. As it gets closer to the most magical time of the year, stores are stocked with decorations big and small, and figuring out how you want your home to look can be a little overwhelming. Thankfully, experts in the home decor space are sharing their seasonal tips to help you get ready.

HGTV’s Jonathan Scott shared a video with a few Christmas decorating hacks he and his partner, Zooey Deschanel, use in their home.

“I like it to be a little bit nostalgic, a little bit fun, and a whole lot of holiday spirit,” Scott says.

There’s no one right way to decorate for Christmas, and even if so that doesn’t mean you should stick to the conventional script, according to Scott. “There are lots of different rules when decorating for the holidays, but of course, as we know, rules are meant to be broken,” Scott says. “So it really depends on your comfort level.”

Even the nicest artificial trees can look a little too perfect. Scott’s trick is to stuff a few extra branches into the tree, leaving some sticking out at random. He also adds more lights, including larger bulbs, even though his tree is already pre-lit.

Scott has been collecting nutcrackers for years, and yes, he even names them. Rather than display them the same way every Christmas, he changes things up with different garlands, beads, and branches. It’s a way to get a new look out of decorations he already owns.

Those giant stacked presents in Scott’s house look like they’d be a pain to store, but they’re not. Each box fits inside the next, so the whole display takes up a fraction of the space once Christmas is over.

You can watch the full video and get more tips here:

At the top of everyone’s mind around the holidays should be safety.

Scott recommends being mindful of fragile decorations, especially if you have young children or large pets. Glass ornaments and other breakable decorations can easily get knocked over, so consider using sturdier pieces in areas where kids and pets spend a lot of time.

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) also recommends looking for a “fire resistant” label when purchasing an artificial Christmas tree and regularly watering live trees to reduce fire risks.

Whether you’re adding a few new touches to your favorite decorations or going all out with a Christmas tree in every room, the most important thing is creating a space that feels festive to you.

#7621. Block, Blunt, Break: NATO’s New Theory of Victory

On October 12, 2026, U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), gave a speech at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland in which he outlined NATO’s new theory of victory to deter and, if necessary, defeat Russian aggression.[REF] This theory of victory, called “Block, Blunt, Break,” centers on employing combined arms and maneuver to block initial enemy assaults on Alliance territory, blunt follow-on offensives, and, if necessary, break the enemy’s ability to sustain combat operations. SACEUR’s speech comes at a time of considerable consternation in Eastern European capitals after months of suspected Russian hybrid activities including drone incursions and sabotage. General Grynkewich’s deterrence-focused theory of victory struck the right tone, reassuring worried allies and signaling to Moscow that the United States and its NATO allies are confident of their ability to defeat a Russian incursion into a NATO state and that Russia would do well not to consider one. The speech and the strategy itself also appear wisely designed to avoid unnecessary escalation with Russia as SACEUR made clear throughout that NATO is a defensive Alliance.

Block, Blunt, Break

General Grynkewich said that a classified version of this new NATO strategy had been agreed on by all 32 members of the Alliance about three months before his October 12 speech.[REF] He explained his decision to present Block, Blunt, Break in public as a helpful measure to assuage increasingly anxious NATO populations vulnerable to evolving security threats.[REF] General Grynkewich summarized his theory of victory as follows: “We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us.”[REF]

Block. NATO land forces will meet any enemy assault with preponderant force at the point of contact and not trade territory for time. As these forces prevent adversaries from seizing Alliance territory, air and sea forces will gain superiority before aggressively supporting NATO forces on the ground. Space and cyber forces will be employed, creating a lattice of forces meant to prevent the enemy from holding its ground.

Blunt. Following the block phase, NATO forces will focus on denying the enemy’s ability to generate offensive momentum. This effort will include expanded deployments of manned and autonomous forces across domains to maintain operational advantage. The mass employment of effects in the forward battlespace will overwhelm enemy formations, thereby disrupting any continued advance.

Break. If the enemy continues its attack or employs reserves, NATO forces will expand operations to break the enemy’s broader warfighting system. NATO will apply mass pressure through all domains to break down the enemy’s ability to sustain its forces. A major contributing factor to this pressure campaign will be the pairing of precision munitions with sweeping volumes of attritable and affordable effects. These efforts will isolate enemy formations from replenishment and paralyze the command and control of the opposing force.[REF]

Strategic Context

This theory of victory is a marked shift from earlier NATO theories of victory, which focused on trading space for time—that is, allowing Russian forces to move into NATO territory, while NATO forces harass and slow Russian advances until decisive force can be brought to bear to destroy and then expel all Russian forces from NATO territory.

Block, Blunt, Break is a significant change from NATO Cold War strategy.

During the Cold War, West Germany was the NATO state considered most likely to be attacked by massive numbers of Soviet-led Warsaw Pact forces, and the Fulda Gap was often identified as the most likely attack route. The geographic size of West Germany meant that NATO forces could fall back tens or hundreds of kilometers before they could generate enough combat mass to begin a counteroffensive against Soviet and Warsaw Pact forces and then expel them from NATO soil. In this sense, NATO planned to trade territory for time, during which it would seize the conventional advantage.

Today, the Suwalki Gap between Lithuania and Poland is often cited as the modern equivalent of the Fulda Gap, especially because it separates Russian-allied Belarus from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.[REF] The three Baltic States of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are for numerous reasons the NATO states against which full-scale Russian aggression is most likely; for example, Russian revanchists claim the existence of Russian-speaking minorities in Estonia and Latvia as a potential pretext, and Russian military planners could seek to connect the Russian exclave by land to either Belarus or Russia, and Lithuania is in their way. In the Baltic States, Block, Blunt, Break makes sense as the strategy for deterring or defending against Russian aggression from both a military planning and a political perspective.

From a military planning perspective, the lack of strategic depth in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania was likely a major factor in the change in strategy. Blocking the Russian advance from the outset prevents the Russians from gaining a foothold that may prove difficult to dislodge once fortified and reinforced.

From a political perspective, Block, Blunt, Break reinforces allied cohesion in the face of Russian aggression against a Baltic state or some other frontline state. Should Russia rapidly gain lodgment within Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, it could then sue for peace before NATO could dislodge Russian forces and liberate those three NATO members. This could well create real political divisions within the North Atlantic Council, in which some countries would press for the liberation of the Baltic States, while others may seek to accept the peace proposal. It is not inconceivable that such a development could lead to the fracturing and potential breakup of NATO—long a goal of Moscow. This new strategy articulated by SACEUR could be a way to defend every inch of NATO soil from the outset and prevent this difficult scenario.

Strategic Signals

General Grynkewich used his speech at the Warsaw Security Forum to demonstrate how NATO allies intend to prevent conflict and defeat aggression if needed. He stressed that NATO’s Block, Blunt, Break strategy is defensive and seeks to prevent enemies from achieving their offensive objectives. While detailing this theory of victory, General Grynkewich provided a vision for a future NATO with enhanced military strength, operational readiness, and a unified commitment to the defense of all the Alliance’s territory.

This speech landed amid persistent suspected Russian gray-zone warfare against European NATO member states. On October 13, Bulgaria’s government summoned the Russian ambassador after two ships were hit by drones near its territorial waters.[REF] Two additional merchant ships were struck by drones near Bulgaria’s coast the week before, attacks that followed a strike on a civilian ship off Romania,[REF] and Romania has faced repeated Russian drone incursions over the past year.[REF]

While not mentioning these and other similar events directly, General Grynkewich stated that threats and intimidation against Alliance members will only bind NATO closer together. He noted that this unity is enhanced by the Alliance’s confidence in its ability to move up the escalation ladder if needed. General Grynkewich identified NATO’s strength, cohesion, and readiness as important factors that should significantly complicate an adversary’s military calculus of escalation. SACEUR also exhorted European NATO allies not to shy away from identifying the source of gray-zone provocations when they occur.

The United States’ ongoing European force posture review and discussions of a likely reduction in U.S. troop levels in Europe as part of the necessary rebalancing of forces to the Indo-Pacific have led to uncertainty among NATO allies regarding America’s contributions to the Alliance.[REF] General Grynkewich’s speech reaffirmed the United States’ commitment to European security, albeit within the larger framework of increased burden sharing promoted by the Trump Administration.

NATO’s theory of victory relies on aggressive, forward resistance to enemy advances. Implementing this operational concept will require the Alliance to bring substantial force to bear within a constrained timeline. While General Grynkewich’s speech serves as an overt commitment to a continued American presence in NATO, European states will likely have to shoulder a significant burden as part of the rapid joint response to an attack on the Alliance. To ensure NATO’s ability to execute this plan, European states should continue expanding their defense spending to improve their warfighting capabilities, forward-deploy certain capabilities, and substantially improve military mobility.

General Grynkewich prefaced his explanation of NATO’s theory of victory with a frank assessment of NATO’s security environment. He held that conflict is neither imminent nor inevitable. This status quo, he said, can be sustained by clearly articulating NATO’s intentions, maintaining open lines of communication with external states, and maintaining deterrence by denial through military capacity.

Commenting on the character of NATO, General Grynkewich stressed that the Alliance is defensive and has “no plans, no intentions, and no ambitions” other than the protection of NATO peoples and territories. SACEUR nevertheless cautioned potential adversaries not to mistake NATO’s defensive nature for a lack of resolve and emphasized that member states will ensure any attack on Alliance territory will prove futile.[REF]

This point was underlined by additional commentary regarding NATO’s deterrence posture. General Grynkewich drew attention to the Alliance’s “decision advantage.” He asserted that NATO will not be caught by surprise thanks to an immense intelligence footprint encompassing a vast network of sensors and sources. General Grynkewich framed NATO’s intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capability as a key enabler of the Alliance’s theory of victory. By rapidly assessing an opposing force’s presence and intent, NATO forces will have time to mobilize in the numbers required to deny attackers at the point of contact, especially because these troops will be reinforcing significant numbers of NATO troops forward positioned within NATO’s easternmost states.

Because of NATO’s doctrine, character, and posture, General Grynkewich remarked that the burden of escalation will always lie upon NATO’s aggressors. NATO’s Block, Blunt, Break strategy seeks only to prevent an enemy from realizing its revisionist aspirations. He plainly asserted that such states will “bear the full moral, political, and strategic weight” of initiating and expanding conflict with the Alliance.[REF]

General Grynkewich included within this posture of deterrence and denial an explicit characterization of NATO’s intentions after the outbreak of conflict. He emphasized that the Alliance’s Block, Blunt, Break strategy does not seek at the outset to impose a strategic defeat upon its adversaries. Instead, NATO seeks simply to employ its theory of victory to maintain the Alliance’s territorial integrity by tactically defeating its attackers.

In sum, General Grynkewich used his speech at the Warsaw Security Forum to communicate fundamental Alliance convictions to audiences both within and outside NATO. He articulated how NATO is not simply relying on decades-old defense strategies but adopting new means to meet emerging security threats. He delineated an internal Alliance dynamic defined by cohesion anchored in a collective determination to defend Alliance territory from opportunistic adversaries. He portrayed to external audiences a NATO whose mandate is limited to protecting its citizens and territory but that is also unified and firm in its willingness to fight and to defeat an aggressor if needed. General Grynkewich confidently messaged to Russia that he wants to assure those who “might be thinking about doing harm against us, that we’ve got this, and that they better not take any shot at the alliance.”[REF]

Wilson Beaver is Senior Policy Advisor for Defense Budgeting and NATO Policy in the Allison Center for National Security at The Heritage Foundation.

#7620. Fifth Circuit Dismisses Lawsuit Over Facebook Removal, Supposedly Connected to Stanford Internet Observatory, of COVID-Related Post

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Hines v. Stamos, decided yesterday by Judges W. Eugene Davis, Leslie Southwick, and Stuart Kyle Duncan:

Jill Hines sued Stanford University, Alex Stamos, and others, alleging they conspired with the government to censor her online speech about COVID-19. The district court dismissed her suit without prejudice for lack of subject-matter and personal jurisdiction. Because Hines has not shown that her injury is fairly traceable to Stanford or Stamos, she lacks standing. We therefore AFFIRM without reaching personal jurisdiction….

This case is closely related to Murthy v. Missouri, which guides our resolution of this appeal. In Murthy, Hines (along with others) sued federal officials and agencies, alleging the government censored her online speech against COVID-19 restrictions in violation of the First Amendment. Here, Hines challenges Defendants' participation in an academic project named the Election Integrity Partnership (EIP). She alleges the EIP and its participants aided the government's scheme to have Facebook suppress her online speech, also in violation of the First Amendment. {Our review is limited to Hines's claims against Stanford and Alex Stamos, the former director of the Stanford Internet Observatory, which was an EIP member.}

Facebook began moderating COVID-19 content early in the pandemic, deleting or demoting posts it deemed false. In April 2020 alone, it labeled roughly 50 million pieces of content. That same month, Hines launched a grassroots campaign to challenge COVID-19 government restrictions and used Facebook to communicate with her supporters. She was aware of Facebook's moderation and took deliberate measures to circumvent it.

The EIP, a consortium of researchers and institutions, was formed in July 2020. It sought to identify misinformation about elections and voting. For about three months in 2020, it monitored elections-related content on social media. EIP participants sometimes recommended actions to social-media platforms and logged their communications when they did. In most instances, the platforms took no detectable action on those recommendations….

To have standing, a "plaintiff must have (1) suffered an injury in fact, (2) that is fairly traceable to the challenged conduct of the defendant, and (3) that is likely to be redressed by a favorable judicial decision." For the claims before us, the second inquiry—traceability of Hines's past injuries—is "the whole ball game." …

There is one injury that Hines claims is traceable to Defendants: on September 9, 2020, Facebook removed a post from Hines's page that attached an article entitled Masks Don't Work. At the time, Facebook explained the post went "against our Community Standards." It also reduced distribution of Hines's page on COVID-19 restrictions for "repeated" violations of its standards on "Inauthentic Behavior" and for "repeated sharing of false news." Hines does not dispute that these restrictions fit Facebook's own content moderation…

Hines's traceability theory rests on an inference drawn from timing. On September 8, 2020, the EIP received a massive submission of over 200 webpages and social-media posts from the Democratic National Committee. Among those 200 webpages was a single post by Hines where she encouraged her followers to lobby their representatives to end the COVID-19 public-health emergency. In Hines's view, the one-day timing between the DNC's submission and Facebook's moderation of her page is evidence that EIP participants called Facebook's attention to her single post in the 200-webpage DNC submission.

We are not persuaded by her argument. Discovery revealed no communication between the EIP and Facebook about Hines, and Facebook did not remove or moderate the post that the EIP received. {Hines argues there may be evidence of Defendants' communications with Facebook in undiscovered Slack or Zoom messages. But Stanford produced "communications and other documents" mentioning Hines or her account, and Hines neither challenged that production nor moved to compel additional discovery, although the scheduling order allowed for that. The mere possibility of undiscovered communications that were not sought in the district court is not evidence.}

A notation in the EIP's records even says Hines's COVID-19 posts were beyond the scope of the EIP's elections-oriented work. We conclude as a matter of law that timing alone is too attenuated to trace Hines's injury to Defendants.

Murthy also requires us to consider Facebook's own incentives to moderate content. Facebook gave its own reasons for acting when it removed Hines's post and demoted her page, and Hines does not dispute that that moderation aligned with Facebook's COVID-19 policies. We agree with the district court that there's no indication that Facebook, in moderating Hines's post, did anything other than follow its own moderation policy….

I am not at all involved with Stanford's defense of this lawsuit.

Elisabeth S. Theodore, John B. Bellinger, III, R. Stanton Jones, and Stephen K. Wirth (Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer, L.L.P.) and James A. Brown (Liskow & Lewis, A.P.L.C.) represent defendants.

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

Our Ratings: Design 5/5; Durability 5/5; Performance 4.5/5; Value 4.5/5

We’re smitten with Belkin’s idea of incorporating pivot plugs in their power strips. What a neat idea! We tested other power strips where the outlets were configured in a way that kept us from using every one of them because using large plugs blocked adjacent outlets. That’s not a problem with pivot plugs.

Turning the outlets one way or the other on the power strip’s column gave us ample space for every plug. Another perk is a clip at the end of the strip where we were able to tuck the cords to help keep things tidy. The Belkin power strip has a heavy-duty 6-foot cord and light-up status indicators that let us know the unit was protected and grounded.

The only downside—and it’s really just a matter of personal preference—is that the power strip itself tends to roll around a bit unless it’s mounted via keyholes on the back. With a high joule rating of 1,800, we think this power strip surge protector is a good pick for sensitive electronics and digital devices.

Get the Belkin PivotPlug 8-outlet power strip at Amazon, Walmart, or Belkin.

Our Ratings: Design 4.5/5; Durability 4.5/5; Performance 5/5; Value 4.5/5

We found a lot to like about the Anker power strip, although it’s more of a square than a strip. It’s a great option for anyone who needs extra plug-ins on the fly. It doesn’t have a joule rating, so it doesn’t provide surge protection; however, it does offer over-volt and short-circuit protection, so we’d be comfortable taking it to an internet cafe, plugging in a laptop, and charging our phone and tablet (via the rapid-charge USB ports) while we work remotely.

We liked the ultra-slim design of this flat plug power strip, which includes a narrow plug that can be plugged into tight spots behind desks and nightstands. While it only offers 2 AC outlets, that’s probably enough for someone traveling or working remotely for the day. It’s not made for plugging in power tools, but it’s perfect for anyone on the go. We also like the fact that it’s made from 75 percent recyclable materials.

Get the Anker power strip at Amazon or Walmart.

Our Ratings: Design 4.5/5; Durability 5/5; Performance 4.5/5; Value 4.3/5

The PowerBox 1 provides 2,160 J of surge protection and comes with magnets on the back for attaching to a metal surface. We liked the idea of the magnets, and they were even stronger than the ones on the DeWalt power strip. We attached the PowerBox to a metal workstand and we had to pull hard just to get it off.

We also liked the mounting holes in all four corners. This allowed us to insert screws to mount the PowerBox to a wall or workbench and eliminate movement. We plugged in large and small plugs with no problems.

Another perk is that this power strip has an 8-foot cord, so it offers more location versatility.

What our tester says: “I think this is a great power strip for use in a home office or media room, where users can plug in several sensitive devices at once without worrying about power surges.”—Glenda Taylor, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Belkin PivotPlug 12-outlet power strip at Amazon or Belkin.

Home office desks are notorious for hosting a messy tangle of cords. Our work desk is covered with cords for speakers, monitors, an Echo Dot, and a mouse. Another cord is involved if we want to charge our phones as we work. As such, we love the organizational ability of this desk-clamp power strip.

It has 5 AC outlets, 2 USB-A ports, and 4 USB-C ports. The clamp is sturdy, and when it’s tightened snugly, it keeps the power strip firmly in place. This is a great little desk power strip, but it isn’t perfect. We solved this problem by plugging the desk power strip into a dedicated surge protector outlet (sold separately) under the desk. It’s the perfect setup for us: outlets in a handy, organized spot, and powerful surge protection for sensitive electronics.

Our Ratings: Design 4/5; Durability 5/5; Performance 4.5/5; Value 4.8/5

Along with a tough build and large capacity, this outdoor power strip is exceptionally well-designed for those who need a power hub for corded power tools. The CRST has a tough aluminum housing that, combined with the thick plastic covers on its ends, makes it capable of enduring plenty of abuse and drops. We appreciated its thicker 14-gauge power cord (most are 16-gauge).

Measuring 15 feet long, the power cord is much longer than others. This allowed us to extend it out into the yard or driveway without having to add an outdoor extension cord. And while that long cord could be unwieldy, the strip includes an integrated cord holder that allowed us to wrap any slack neatly around the housing and secure it with a Velcro strap. If you need a power strip with a long cord, this is the one.

Its bright yellow color makes it more visible to foot traffic, and it comes equipped with a 15-amp breaker switch in case the user pulls too much juice at one time. This is a good power strip for outdoor DIY projects, but it’s not water-resistant, so use it only in dry conditions.

When we started researching the best power strips, we discovered hundreds of different options on the market, so we started by looking carefully at the top-rated models. We took brand names into consideration, to an extent—Anker and Belkin are well-respected names in the industry, for example—but we also looked carefully at niche brands and AmazonBasics picks with good customer reviews. Our initial list had over 35 best-selling power strips, but we narrowed that down to 15 picks we wanted to try out for ourselves.

In our hands-on testing, we used the power strips for two weeks, noting their build quality, trying out their features, and assessing their design. We plugged in battery chargers, power tools, PCs, monitors, peripherals, and small appliances.

Since the primary purpose of buying a power strip is to have additional outlets, we noted how easy (or difficult) it was to use all of the outlets on the strip at the same time. Our goal wasn’t to see how much power we could pull—that depends solely on the circuit—but to see how well the strips were designed for real-world use.

We awarded points based on a rubric: the better a strip performed on a test or assessment, the higher the points. After testing, we averaged the points to find our top pick and categorize the others by their best use.

Before choosing the best power strip for your needs, consider how and where you plan to use it, as well as the important factors below.

The right power strip for your needs depends heavily on how it will be used and which devices or equipment will be plugged into it.

The number of outlets you need in a power strip depends on both how many and what type of devices you want to plug into it. Remember that you should not plug high-power-capacity devices into power strips, regardless of the number of outlets. The circuit still limits the power strip.

Power strips can have as few as two outlets or more than 20. These outlets can be standard power outlets, USB-A or USB-C outlets, wide-spaced outlets intended for larger adapters, and specialty connections like ethernet or coaxial connections. The number and configuration of outlets are mostly a personal preference; however, consider that as the number of outlets increases, so does the size of the power strip. So, if space is an issue, choose a power strip with fewer outlets and a narrower profile.

Length and configuration refer to the length of the cord and the type of outlets in the power strip.

In our technologically advanced society, many devices and appliances embedded with complex electrical systems are very sensitive to power surges, so surge protection is a feature of a power strip nearly everyone needs. Power surges typically occur when a storm brings down electrical lines, causing the power company to reroute power to address power demands. These changes can create inconsistent power flow fluctuations, resulting in a power surge. The only way to protect all appliances and devices is with a whole-house surge protector, but strips with surge protection will reduce the risk of damage to sensitive electronics and devices.

Surge protection—also referred to as the surge suppression rating of a power strip—is measured in joules (J) and normally varies, depending on the product, from as low as 100 J to higher than 4,000 J. When using a power strip as surge protection for expensive or sensitive devices, it is important to invest in a power strip with a high surge suppression rating.

A standard power strip runs electricity to multiple devices, typically via an on/off switch. Smart power strips function similarly, but they can also connect with compatible smart home systems, like Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant, usually through a WiFi connection.

Once a smart power strip connects to a smart home system, users can control the electrical supply to the paired devices through either voice control or a smartphone app. Some power strips even support timers or schedules so connected devices will automatically turn on or off.

While power strips don’t seem very dangerous, cords can become trip hazards and electrocution and fires can result from improper use. Many power strip manufacturers include safety features like full-metal housing, internal circuit breakers, or ground-fault circuit interrupters (GFCIs) to protect users and their property from harm.

Take a look below to find the answers to some of the most commonly asked questions about electrical power outlet strips.

If used properly, a power strip can actually reduce the risk of electrical fire by providing a safe place to plug in additional accessories. However, if misused, either by overloading it, using it for appliances it’s not rated for, or linking multiple power strips together (called daisy-chaining), a power strip can become a danger.

Never plug high-power-capacity appliances, such as electric space heaters, refrigerators, microwaves, toaster ovens, and air conditioners, into a power strip.

Daisy-chaining power strips means linking multiple power strips together in a series that connects back to a single electrical outlet. This is a big concern for fire-fighting professionals because daisy-chained connections will almost invariably lead to an overloaded power strip that heats up until it burns out or catches fire.

Power strips can catch fire if they are old or frayed, or if they are overloaded beyond their capacity. This can happen when several devices that draw too much electricity, such as air conditioners or electric heaters, are plugged into the same strip. The strip will then heat up and eventually begin to melt, sparking a fire.

While there is some discrepancy between specific products, on average, power strips will last for about 2 years before replacement is necessary. However, they can last between 3 to 5 years if properly maintained.

It depends on what you plug into the strips, but in general, it’s not a good practice to plug two strips into one outlet. Overloading the circuit will cause the breaker to trip.

In a home that has too few outlets for the owners’ needs, power strips can absolutely be worth the money because they expand the number of outlets available. Power strips that have surge protection are also ideal for homes with a lot of sensitive electronics, as the strips prevent damage when power surges might otherwise cause damage. Just keep in mind that power strips don’t actually provide more power to the home—they just allow more devices to use the power that’s already there.

It’s not a bad idea. Turning it off will reduce standby energy usage, but as long as you’re not overloading the circuit, it should be safe to leave on.

Recliners for seniors are designed with comfort and mobility in mind. Traditional recliners have a cozy, enveloping design, but this can make them difficult to sit down in and stand up from. For seniors, power lift recliners solve this problem by having a lifting mechanism that lifts the chair to them.

These motorized chairs are much easier to get in and out of. Ideal for seniors and individuals with mobility concerns, they are safer to use and place less strain on stiff or aching joints. Selecting the right furniture and design elements for one’s home isn’t easy—especially when it comes to keeping our elderly loved ones comfortable and safe. But we found a few products we think stand above others, such as our overall favorite, the Ashley Furniture Yandel Power Lift Recliner. It’s a well-rounded option suitable for all types of homes thanks to its classic look, and more importantly, it’s comfortable and easy to use. Ahead, learn about the best recliners for seniors that are comfortable, practical, and safe, allowing seniors to relax with ease.

Bottom line: Power lift recliners provide comfort and mobility for seniors, with top picks offering features like massage and heat for enhanced relaxation.

For seniors and those with mobility limitations, lift recliners provide all the comfort of a traditional recliner while being easier to get in and out of. The cozy picks ahead are easy to use and comfortable to allow more time for relaxing or napping.

For even more comfort, this manual reclining chair has a pull handle to provide users with a smooth and quiet recline. We like the versatility this allows, as the user can adjust the incline angle precisely to their liking. If you’re looking for a compact recliner, this lift recliner from Mcombo is a suitable pick. And while it isn’t exactly a heavy-duty recliner, it does boast a high weight capacity of up to 320 pounds, so it’s capable of carrying more weight than other comparable chairs.

Still, Mcombo recommends this lift recliner for individuals ranging from 4 feet 6 inches to 5 feet 2 inches tall. It’s an excellent choice for petite people who might feel swallowed up by larger recliners, which can make them harder to stand from, even with a lifting feature. This recliner is a single-motor option that features three positions (reclined, partially reclined, and lifted). Lift recliners can make it easier and safer for elderly individuals to get in and out of a recliner. We focused on the priorities that every person wants from any type of chair, so the chairs on this list needed to be comfortable, practical, and safe. We considered product specifications and consumer reviews to narrow down this list from more than 20 recliner options.

We also spoke with Dr. Logan DuBose, the co-founder of Olera Care, a nationwide community platform for connecting family caregivers to service providers in the senior care industry, funded by the National Institute on Aging. He shared some thoughts about the struggles seniors go through and how these impact the products designed for them: “Seniors frequently grapple with physical limitations, including diminished hand strength, coordination, and joint stiffness. Conditions like Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s, dementia, or neuropathy can compound these challenges.” He went on to say that typical motions younger folks would take for granted “become notably difficult, presenting formidable obstacles.”

As such, safety is paramount when it comes to any product, but especially when used by those with limited mobility. We looked for smooth-moving chairs with an ergonomic design and a decent weight capacity to suit most users.

Recliners for seniors also need to be easy to control—no one should have to fiddle around with a complicated remote just to get out of a chair. To ensure these criteria were met, we chose highly reviewed products with user-friendly controls.

We looked for comfortable and stylish designs with ample padding and a shape that envelops the body for ultimate relaxation. The lift chairs on this list also look nice, with attractive designs, textures, and colors. We chose from a range of colors and materials to suit different shopper preferences.

After a long day, sinking into your favorite recliner is a welcome treat. But for those who find getting into a favorite chair harder than usual, it might be time to invest in a recliner for seniors. The best recliners for elderly individuals feature mobility aids that make it easier to get in and out of a cushy seat. When choosing these recliners, consider the recliner type, motor size, material, and additional functions.

While all recliners can be suitable for seniors, some have extra features that make them easier to use. For seniors with full mobility, traditional, swivel, massaging, and rocker recliners are all comfortable picks. These chairs can be manual or electric; electric options may be easier to use for those with any mobility concerns. But if getting in and out of a recliner is harder than it used to be, consider a lifting recliner.

Lift recliners are essentially recliners engineered to lift the user with minimal manual effort required. Designed for those who have a hard time sitting down or standing up from a seated position, they use a power mechanism to raise the chair up. They look the same as traditional recliners, but the lifting mechanism makes them a popular choice for seniors.

Lift recliners come in single-motor or dual-motor designs. As the name suggests, single-motor chairs have one motor that controls the chair’s entire range of movement, powering both the lifting mechanism and reclining mechanism. These chairs are less adjustable but tend to be more affordable than dual-motor chairs. Most single-motor lift chairs have one button that operates the lift and one that operates both the recliner and the footrest as one piece, so when you recline the chair, the footrest follows in a preset position.

Dual-motor chairs have two motors that power different parts of the chair. One motor controls the recline angle, while the other controls the footrest and lifting mechanism. This design allows for infinite positioning, so you can adjust each independently to find your perfect lounging position.

Recliners can take up a fair amount of space in a room, so it’s important to consider the chair dimensions when shopping. Space is especially a concern for lift recliners, which tend to be larger and heavier than standard recliners on account of their motors and parts.

Due to their reclining design, recliners also need enough space behind and in front of them to fully extend. Before you start shopping, measure your space to make sure the recliner can fit without hitting the wall or any other chairs or tables.

Besides considering the room space, make sure the recliner is a suitable size for your needs. Most recliners will advertise their weight capacity, which should not be exceeded, especially in the case of lift recliners. Tall users may opt for a longer chair for better comfort. Choose a recliner that is suitable for both the user’s height and weight.

Recliner frames can be made of plywood, hardwood, or metal. Metal is generally the sturdiest option, and lift recliners tend to use a mix of wood and metal to create a durable frame. These materials have the strength to support the chair (and the user’s body) as it lifts, but keep in mind that each lift recliner will have a weight limit that should be followed.

Recliner cushions for elderly people can be made of foam, memory foam, down, or an innerspring system. Combined with an ergonomic design, any of these materials can offer a comfortable seat. Upholstery options can vary across a range of materials, which are explored ahead.

Upholstered recliners come in a variety of materials. The most popular materials include fabric, leather, and vinyl. Look for an option that is comfortable, breathable, and easy to clean.

Fabrics are among the softest options and come in a range of colors, textures, and materials. This category includes cotton, polyester, microfiber, microsuede, and performance fabrics. High-quality fabrics are durable and breathable, but they can stain and absorb spills. Leather (whether real or fake) and vinyl make for easy-to-clean, smooth chair covers. While they aren’t as plush or breathable as fabrics, leather and vinyl chairs come in a variety of colors and have a sleek look.

Beyond comfort, consider ease of cleaning when choosing a recliner material. The best recliners for elderly users are easy to clean. Due to their weave, fabrics tend to be the toughest to clean, while smooth materials like leather and vinyl are easy to wipe down.

Lifted recliners for elderly users tend to have a roomy and comfortable design with well-stuffed cushions. Like traditional recliners, they’re made for relaxing, but they also have the addition of a mobility aid.

Beyond lifting up and down to get the user out of the chair, the best power lift recliner chairs also offer reclining abilities and footrests for lounging. When choosing a comfortable pick, consider the reclining angle, which can range from 140 degrees to almost 180 degrees.

Design can be just as important as comfort. Recliners can take up a fair amount of space in a living room or a bedroom, so you’ll want a choice that looks nice in your space. Lift recliners look like regular recliners and come in a wide range of colors, materials, and designs, so you can find one that suits your style.

Lift recliners are popular for seniors and those with mobility issues, and for good reason. These comfortable recliners can help those with limited mobility by making it easier to sit and stand at just the touch of a button. When activated, they lift and angle the recliner to put the user as close to a standing position as possible and make the chair easier to get in and out of.

Power lift recliners include a remote control or a control panel to make adjustments. In most chairs, all their features are automated to make them easier for seniors to use. Control options can include lifting the chair, reclining the back, opening the footrest, and switching on any heat or massage modes.

Massage and heat settings add even more comfort to a lift recliner. Massage recliners feature rollers or parts inside the chair that either knead or vibrate to create a massaging motion. These are commonly distributed across the backrest, but some chairs offer massage zones that also target different parts of the back area, thighs, and legs. Massage recliners can have one massage mode or varying intensities and massage types.

Lift recliners often offer heating functions that offer pleasant warming sensations. These features can help with sore or aching muscles and joints, or, more simply, help the user create a cozy cocoon for relaxing or napping. Heating zones can target different areas of the body.

Lift recliners for seniors can come with additional bells and whistles for a better seating experience. Storage areas can keep devices and other items within easy reach and ready for use, and charging ports are another useful perk.

Cup holders are a common and obvious feature; they’re made to hold your drinks but can also be used to hold other items. For added storage, some recliners also feature arm storage pockets to hold remotes, cables, and books. USB ports are a useful addition that allow the user to charge devices while relaxing.

Products for seniors need to be easy to use, and lift recliners are no exception. When it comes to a large item like a lift recliner, ease of use also contributes to safety. The best power lift recliner options are designed with seniors in mind, so they’re a safe option to have around the home.

Most are controlled using a control panel or a corded remote control, so adjusting their settings is as simple as pushing a button—the chair will do the rest. The control panel or remote is often used for more than the lifting feature, also controlling the recline angle and footrest. A high-quality lift recliner will move slowly and smoothly to allow users to gain their footing.

Lift recliners are one of the best recliners for seniors and individuals with limited mobility. They are essentially recliners that lift you up, making it easier to lower into the seat or stand from a seated position.

Lift recliners look and feel the same as traditional recliners, so they have all the comfort perks of a regular recliner, with the added benefit of a mobility aid. Since lift recliners are electric-powered, they are also very easy to use. With the press of a button or the flick of a switch, users can adjust them to their liking.

Beyond being easy to use, lift recliners are also a safe addition. Sitting down and standing from a low seat (like many traditional recliners) can be difficult for stiff or achy joints, and it can even create a fall hazard for some individuals. A lift recliner can help seniors safely maintain their freedom and independence for longer.

While any recliner may be suitable for seniors, lift recliners are one of the best options. Even if you don’t have mobility concerns, lift recliners for elderly citizens can offer a bit of extra support for aching bones and joints. Still deciding on the best recliner for your needs? Read on for some frequently asked questions and answers about recliners for seniors.

For seniors, a seat height between 17 and 18 inches is often ideal, but this varies with the size of the user.

Also known as a “geri” chair, a geriatric recliner is a large, padded reclining chair on casters, usually used in senior living facilities or hospital settings. They provide great seated comfort and support and can be wheeled to adjoining areas with ease.

Some geriatric chairs can be fully reclined for sleeping; however, it’s safer and generally more comfortable to sleep in a bed.

When the chair is in a reclined position, your heel should hang slightly over the end of the footrest. If your feet hang too far off the recliner footrest, it’s best to find a longer pick; this positioning can put uncomfortable pressure on the back of your legs.

Look for a quality recliner that is supportive and fully adjustable so that the user can find the best position to soothe a painful back.

Medicare or Medicaid may cover some of the costs for a lift chair if it is considered medically necessary. It’s best to consult with a doctor or Medicare or Medicaid provider to see if your situation is eligible.

#7617. Does Board and Management Diversity Improve Financial Performance? The Evidence Is Weak

In 1954, the economist Darrell Huff published How to Lie with Statistics, a slim volume that became, improbably, one of the best-selling statistics books in American publishing history. Huff’s central insight—that correlation dressed in the vestments of causation can seduce even careful readers—has aged better than most mid-century paperbacks. It’s due for a revival.

Especially in the wake of a new report, Capturing the Diversity Benefit, which claims that companies with more racially diverse management teams perform better financially.

The report is not without ambition. It draws on federal EEO-1 workforce filings matched to financial data for 1,482 publicly traded companies between 2016 and 2024, and it contains some genuine quantitative analysis.

But its empirical research design is deeply flawed, and in ways Huff would have recognized instantly. The analysis may document correlations inside a selected dataset, but it does not establish that management diversity improves corporate performance, that DEI programs create shareholder value, or that companies incur financial risk by scaling those programs back.

Consider, first, the sample, always the place a skeptical reader should look, and always the place such reports hope one will not. The number of observed companies changes substantially by year, reaching 1,059 workforce observations in 2020 and falling to 523 in 2024. Earlier data combine voluntary disclosures with records obtained through a Department of Labor Freedom of Information Act release. Later data rely heavily on voluntary disclosure alone, a shift roughly analogous to switching, mid-poll, from a mandatory census to a call for volunteers.

>>> DEI’s Days in the Corporate World Are Numbered

The report itself concedes the consequence: companies choosing to disclose had 4.5 percentage points more BIPOC management representation than companies that never disclosed. Selection into the sample is therefore entangled with the very variable under study, which is a polite way of saying the study measures, in part, itself.

Nor does the report tell readers how its companies compare with the Russell 3000 or the CRSP-Compustat universe, the benchmarks against which any claim to represent “corporate America” must be tested. Readers do not learn whether the sample differs in size, industry, age, profitability, exchange listing, geographic exposure, or prior stock performance.

These are not incidental details; they are precisely the characteristics that predict both workforce composition and financial outcomes. Pooling a large technology company with a small regional manufacturer and regressing profits on a single demographic measure does not make those differences disappear. It merely makes them invisible.

The changing sample, moreover, weakens whatever trends the report reports. An average can move for two quite different reasons: because the same firms changed, or because different firms wandered into and out of the dataset. To its credit, the report acknowledges that sample composition may explain part of the sharp decline in female representation it reports for financial services between 2020 and 2021.

That caveat, once granted, applies throughout the time series, a fact the report is less eager to grant. A balanced panel and a decomposition of within-firm change from sample entry and exit are prerequisites, not refinements, for interpreting these averages as corporate trends rather than statistical artifacts of who happened to show up.

Measurement supplies a second problem, and a subtler one. EEO-1 filings are more standardized than ordinary ESG ratings, which is a modest compliment, but they still require decisions about establishments, corporate ownership, mergers, missing filings, and the aggregation of executive, senior, first-line, and mid-level managers. The report provides too little information to reproduce those choices. Its Racial Justice Initiative score is even less transparent. It combines 27 indicators—ranging from promotion data and EEO-1 disclosure to public statements, donations, and references to political movements—with some categories assigned five times the weight of others. One is invited to trust the recipe without seeing the kitchen.

The ESG measurement literature explains, with some precision, why these choices matter. Florian Berg, Julian Kölbel, and Roberto Rigobon compared six major ESG rating systems and found correlations ranging from 0.38 to 0.71, hardly the tight clustering one would expect if these systems were measuring the same underlying reality. They attribute 56% of rating divergence to measurement, 38% to scope, and 6% to weighting.

Any claimed DEI-performance relationship therefore raises a prior question, one the report never quite gets around to asking: What DEI score is being used, which indicators enter it, and how are they weighted? A composite social score cannot be treated as an objective corporate trait without its coding rules, missing-data procedures, reliability checks, and sensitivity to alternative weights. Put simply, DEI and ESG scores vary so markedly across providers that they have largely lost their meaning as fixed facts about a company.

Related research by Christos Makridis and Majeed Simaan demonstrates that this measurement noise is not merely an academic nuisance; it has real consequences for actual investment decisions. Using more than 22,000 firm-year observations and 21 years of out-of-sample portfolio tests, they find that portfolios incorporating Refinitiv ESG scores do not consistently outperform return-based strategies on a risk-adjusted basis. ESG-only rules can produce higher average returns in some specifications, true enough, but they also generate greater volatility and downside risk (the fine print investors are seldom shown).

Return-based factor models achieve comparable or better ex-post ESG standing without using ESG ratings directly at all. Their panel analysis also finds that market volatility predicts later ESG ratings, while ESG ratings do not predict later volatility, suggesting the ratings absorb information the market already knew rather than furnishing anything so useful as foresight.

Capturing the Diversity Benefit then commits its largest error, and here Huff would surely have reached for his red pen: it estimates simple bivariate regressions. Financial performance depends on firm size, book-to-market ratios, profitability, investment, leverage, industry, firm age, prior performance, and macroeconomic conditions. The main analysis controls for none of them. This omission is especially damaging because the report’s own tables show sharply different results across market-capitalization groups. The authors call firm size “almost certainly” a confound—then proceed, undeterred, to present unadjusted aggregate estimates anyway.

Income after tax, measured in dollars, illustrates the difficulty. Large companies generally earn more dollars and may also employ more diverse managers. A positive coefficient can therefore capture company scale rather than operating performance—correlation masquerading, once again, as insight.

Raw multiyear stock-price appreciation is similarly inadequate to the task. Finance researchers evaluate abnormal returns only after accounting for established sources of risk and return. The Fama-French five-factor model incorporates market exposure, size, value, profitability, and investment; cross-sectional work commonly employs the Fama-MacBeth method to test whether a given characteristic predicts returns after competing explanations have had their say. The report employs none of this.

Timing presents yet another serious obstacle. Matching workforce composition in a given year with performance measured in that same year does not reveal which came first. Strong companies may simply have more resources to recruit broadly, invest in management systems, and publish workforce data in the first place. Both diversity and performance may reflect nothing more exotic than management quality itself. Showing that a correlation existed before 2020 does not resolve the question of reverse causality. It merely pushes it back a few years. At a minimum, the analysis should use lagged representation to predict future outcomes, control for prior performance, and account for the swath of unobserved differences across firms over time.

The report also runs hundreds of statistical tests across demographic groups—approximately 15 outcomes, 11 sectors, three size categories, and nine years. At a 5% significance threshold, false positives become not merely possible but inevitable when researchers search across that many combinations. It would be more surprising if nothing turned up significant by chance alone. Yet the tables display only plus signs, minus signs, and blanks. They omit coefficients, standard errors, confidence intervals, and economic magnitudes—the very information a reader would need to judge whether “significant” means “large” or merely “detectable.” The analysis should identify a small set of primary outcomes and adjust for multiple testing accordingly.

Prior research illustrates why this quantitative discipline matters so greatly. Jeremiah Green and John Hand attempted to reproduce McKinsey’s influential diversity-performance findings using observable S&P 500 data and found no statistically reliable relationship between executive racial and ethnic diversity and industry-adjusted profitability, sales growth, return on assets, return on equity, or total shareholder return. Their critique also identifies reverse causality in relating later diversity measures to earlier performance—the chicken-and-egg problem dressed in academic clothing.

>>> The Myth of “Voluntary” ESG

Alex Edmans, Caroline Flammer, and Simon Glossner draw an equally important conceptual distinction. Their employee-survey measure of DEI has little correlation with demographic representation as such. It is associated with stronger future accounting performance, earnings surprises, and valuation ratios while demographic diversity, on its own, is not. The DEI measure also does not predict future stock returns. Representation, inclusion, and corporate programs are, in short, different constructs measuring different things, and the report moves among them with a freedom the evidence does not license.

Which raises the damning question: if DEI scores do not reliably reflect a company’s actual demographic composition, doesn’t the entire argument collapse under its own premise?

None of this forecloses the possibility that a serious analysis might yet find that management diversity contains financially relevant information. The current report has simply not demonstrated it. The authors should compare their sample with the public-company universe, publish their data construction and coding rules, use a balanced panel, estimate models with firm and year fixed effects, control for standard company characteristics, evaluate factor-adjusted returns, lag the workforce variables, and correct for multiple testing. They should also report effect sizes rather than colored symbols, which are decorative rather than dispositive.

Until then, the defensible conclusion is a modest one: among the company-years observed in this selectively disclosed dataset, some measures of management representation correlate with some financial outcomes. That could well be the case. But it does not establish a “diversity benefit,” and the distance between those two claims is the whole of the matter. Corporate leaders should demand better evidence before accepting a financial claim simply because it supports a preferred social or political conclusion. The same standard, it hardly needs saying, should apply when the conclusion cuts in the opposite direction. Huff, one suspects, would have appreciated the symmetry.

Drafty windows, cold walls and rising heating bills? The RISION Magic Series helps you spot potential trouble areas before they become expensive problems.

Sponsored By: RISIONThis piece was created in partnership with RISION, your go-to for thermal imaging cameras and smart sensing devices.

Imagine cranking up the thermostat on a freezing winter morning to get cozy, only to find that somehow your living room still feels chilly. Maybe there’s a draft coming from the windows, or one area never seems to warm up. Whatever the reason, you might be heating a home that’s letting the warmth escape—and paying through the nose for it.

According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s ENERGY STAR program, you can save an average of 15% on heating and cooling costs by sealing air leaks and adding insulation where it’s needed. The tricky part? Figuring out exactly where the problems are.

That’s where a thermal imaging camera comes in handy. Instead of guessing which windows need resealing or where insulation might be missing, you can use one to spot temperature differences and take a closer look.

I recently got my hands on both the RISION Magic and Magic Pro thermal cameras and spent time with them around my house. Better yet, both models are on sale for up to 45% off during Black Friday sales, making now an excellent time to pick one up.

A thermal imaging camera detects infrared radiation emitted by objects and turns this into a visual representation of surface temperatures. Warmer (red, orange) and cooler (blue, purple) areas appear in contrasting colors, allowing you to see temperature differences that you can’t see with your own eyes.

This opens up some useful possibilities for homeowners. Imagine scanning around a window and spotting a cooler section along the frame. That doesn’t automatically mean there’s an air leak, but it’s a good reason to check the weatherstripping, caulking or surrounding insulation.

You can also use thermal imaging to check on other common household issues:

But remember: thermal imaging isn’t a crystal ball. There can be several reasons for surface temperature differences, and the camera won’t tell you exactly what’s wrong behind a wall. Still, it can help narrow down the places worth checking out before you start ripping off trim or making repairs.

That’s the appeal of the RISION Magic Series. The camera plugs directly into a compatible USB-C smartphone, tablet or computer, so there’s no need to carry around a bulky device. This thing is about the size of a packet of mints.

I spent a couple of days with the RISION Magic and Magic Pro, and one of my favorite things about these cameras is how little effort it takes to get started.

There’s no tiresome setup process or annoying account registration. I took the camera out of its box, plugged it into my phone, downloaded the app and started viewing the thermal feed. The whole process took less than two minutes. Considering how many devices require an email address, password and account verification before you can use them, this was a refreshing change.

The app itself is just as straightforward. You get a live thermal image and simple buttons to capture a photo or record a video. That’s about all there is to it, and that’s all you really need.

I was super impressed by the camera’s sensitivity. As I walked around my house, I could actually see the residual warmth of my footprints on the carpet. Plugged-in electronics appeared as warm spots, while my air-conditioning vents stood out in deep blue against the warmer ceiling.

The app also automatically highlighted particularly hot and cold areas with temperature readouts, making it easy to identify points of interest without constantly examining the entire image. Every now and then, the hotter readouts were difficult to read because the red writing was so close to the red heat source, but a little shift in camera angle normally fixes it.

Editor’s note: Both cameras require a compatible USB-C device and RISION’s accompanying software. They do not support Lightning connectors.

The RISION Magic is a great entry point if you’re looking to investigate insulation problems, cold spots or other temperature-related issues around the house. As someone who’s occasionally had trouble getting consistent readings from traditional stud finders, I found this useful, though I’d still confirm stud locations before drilling.

I also scanned around my windows, looking for cold spots that might indicate gaps in the seals or in the surrounding insulation. Thankfully, I didn’t find any major areas of concern. My house is only about two years old, so that was reassuring.

The Magic makes this type of inspection quick and easy, even if you have no previous experience with thermal cameras.

For a regular homeowner, the extra resolution could be useful during larger renovation projects or more thorough home inspections. But the real appeal is for contractors, HVAC technicians, appliance repair professionals and experienced DIYers who want more information from their thermal images.

One unexpectedly useful application I found while testing was identifying cooler patches on carpeting. #7615. Nina and the Bikers

There were two springs, back when my brother and I were still boys of that gawky middle-school age, when my grandparents, Nina and Papa, gathered us up and carried us west. I have come to think of those two trips as a single, long unspooling of memory.

The first took us to Arizona. We saw the Grand Canyon, that impossible gash in the earth, and the Painted Desert beyond it, striped like something bruised and beautiful. We bounced along in the backs of jeeps that kicked up desert dust. We stayed at a hotel in Flagstaff, where the mornings came on white with snow and the afternoons turned hot and dry as a stovetop, as though the day couldn’t decide what season it wanted to be.

The second spring we went to Jackson Hole, to the Tetons standing up out of the earth like something out of scripture, and there we stayed in a log cabin, where the rangers warned us, upon arrival, of a moose grown ill-tempered from guests who wouldn’t leave him be. Naturally, I took this admonition as an invitation. While Nina sat rocking on the porch, drinking in the view with a contentment only a woman of her years could summon, I crept beneath the floorboards and began to stomp and snort and generally conjure, as best I understood it, the sound of an enraged and antlered beast.

She shrieked; I laughed.

>>> Poe, the Pandemic and a Halloween Lesson for Catholics and Protestants

From there we went to Yellowstone, to Old Faithful and the moose that actually behaved themselves. I remember, at the geyser, an old man off to the side smoking a pipe, the smoke curling up thin and blue against all that steam, and Papa remarking, almost wistfully, on how good it smelled. Nina said he ought to have one himself if he wanted it so badly, then waved the thought away before it could take root.

It was only later that I learned the truth of it: that Papa had given up his pipe before his own sons were born—my uncles, twins, identical down to the part in their hair—because he hadn’t wanted them growing up believing it an admirable habit. This was long before anyone had made a campaign of such things. He had simply decided it, alone, the way men of his generation did, and never smoked again.

We went white-water rafting down the Snake River, my brother and I giddy with anticipation, having not yet learned to factor our grandparents’ ages into our adventures. It turned out to be less a plunge through rapids than a gentle float past serene banks, the water flat and shining as poured glass. And it was later that day, pulled over at some highway overlook to admire the view, that the bikers came: a great, leather-clad, tattooed gang of them, thundering up out of nowhere until it was only them and us. My brother and I did the arithmetic of our own mortality and did not like the sum.

But Nina—devout as she was, pious in a manner that never once announced itself—had already seen the little fish symbol stamped on one of the motorcycles, and before either of us could stop her, she was walking straight toward them, unhurried, as if she’d been expecting them all along. We were certain she would die.

>>> A Very Merry Southern Christmas

Instead, within moments, she was praying with them, the whole rough, tattooed circle of them bowed together on the roadside, and then there was laughter, and embracing, and finally—this being the age of disposable cameras—photographs, Nina beaming in the middle of hairy, greasy men who just before had looked to us like the end of the world.

That photograph exists somewhere still, I have to believe, though my grandmother died last year, and it has not yet turned up.

Adam Smith, in closing his Theory of Moral Sentiments, observed something of how swiftly we render our verdicts upon strangers, how a glance, a coat, a scar, a rough voice, can convict a man in an instant, long before he has said a word in his own defense. It’s sympathy alone, he thought, that corrects the error, the strange and sudden capacity to feel our way into another’s situation and find, waiting there, not the stranger we feared but the neighbor we hadn’t yet recognized.

I think of my grandmother on that roadside, walking toward the very thing my brother and I had already convicted, carrying no evidence but a small fish stamped in chrome—and finding exactly what Smith promised was always there to be found, if only someone was brave enough, or faithful enough, to go looking for it before the verdict came.
